outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the entire survey paper. It will outline the rapid evolution of LLM security threats from 2023 to 2026, covering training-time vulnerabilities (data and model poisoning), inference-time exploits (adversarial attacks and prompt injection), and output reliability issues (hallucinations). The abstract will highlight the paradigm shift from simple text-based exploits to complex vulnerabilities in autonomous agents and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), summarizing key defense strategies and future directions.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: This section introduces the motivation and scope of the survey, detailing the rapid and sophisticated evolution of the LLM security landscape between 2023 and 2026. It will outline the transition from early prompt-based exploits and basic factual errors to deep architectural vulnerabilities, autonomous agent weaponization, and reasoning-level poisoning. The introduction will clearly define the scope of the survey, summarizing the contributions and providing a roadmap for the subsequent sections, emphasizing the critical need for robust alignment and defense mechanisms in both standard LLMs and emerging Large Reasoning Models (LRMs).

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section establishes the foundational concepts and terminology used throughout the survey. It will define key terms such as Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct vs. Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Hallucination. Furthermore, it will provide a brief overview of LLM architectures, including the recent emergence of Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). Finally, it will present a comprehensive threat model overview, distinguishing between training-time threats (e.g., poisoning) and inference-time threats (e.g., adversarial attacks, prompt injection).

outline.title: 3. Data and Model Poisoning: Training-Time Vulnerabilities
outline.description: This section covers the evolution of data and model poisoning from 2023 to 2026. It will begin with early 2024 research demonstrating the fragility of RLHF and DPO, specifically how preference datasets can be manipulated via label-flipping to compromise reward models [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF, Kusaka_2025_LLM]. It will explore the expansion of poisoning into specialized domains like code generation [Yan_2024_LLM, Hossen_2024_Double] and multilingual contexts where backdoors transfer across languages [He_2024_LLMs]. Crucially, it will detail the 2025 paradigm shift toward 'behavioral' and 'reasoning' poisoning in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), demonstrating how the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be hijacked to induce deceptive reasoning or force logical step-skipping [Zhu_2025_Think, Shen_2025_Decepchain].

outline.title: 4. Adversarial Attacks on LLMs
outline.description: This section details the progression of adversarial attacks from simple exploits to deep architectural vulnerabilities. It will start with foundational 2023 work on targeted data poisoning in natural language-to-code generators via 'reverse code repair' [Improta_2023_AI]. It will then cover 2024 advancements in white-box analysis tools measuring backdoor triggers in neuron activations and embeddings [Cheng_2024_Unit, Hussain_2024_Measuring, Nguyen_2024_Pbp]. The section will also address interaction-based vulnerabilities exploiting multi-turn conversational history [Hao_2024_Exploring] and 'context-shifting' strategies bypassing guardrails via expert programming contexts [Noever_2024_AI]. Finally, it will highlight 2025 trends focusing on autonomous agents, specifically the susceptibility of the ReAct framework to control-flow hijacking and autonomous CVE exploitation.

outline.title: 5. Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section explores the rapid evolution of prompt injection (PI) and jailbreaking between 2024 and 2026. It will discuss early 2024 structural and formatting vulnerabilities, such as 'FlipAttack' [Liu_2024_Flipattack] and 'AutoDan' [Liu_2024_Autodan], which exploited autoregressive properties, alongside automated black-box generation frameworks using evolutionary algorithms [Zhao_2024_SQL]. The narrative will then shift to the 2025 paradigm shift toward complex, autonomous agentic systems, investigating Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in multi-modal environments like web navigation and coding editors [Shi_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_Webinject, Johnson_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, it will analyze new vulnerabilities introduced by 'Reasoning LLMs' (RLLMs) like DeepSeek-R1, specifically targeting their internal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes [Cui_2025_LLM, Cui_2025_LLMs].

outline.title: 6. LLM Hallucinations and Factual Inconsistencies
outline.description: This section examines the transition from basic factual error detection to deep mechanistic auditing of LLM hallucinations (2024-2026). It will cover 2024 foundational work on visual hallucinations in Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), specifically the 'language prior' problem [Wang_2024_Mllm, Xing_2024_Mitigating], and the rise of Natural Language Inference (NLI) for factual consistency checking [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative]. The section will highlight 2025 advancements demonstrating that specialized small-scale models (3.8B to 8B parameters) can match or exceed GPT-4 in hallucination detection [Ivry_2025_Paladin, Yaron_2025_GPT, Paudel_2025_Hallucinot]. It will also explore the expansion into multilingual contexts [Islam_2025_LLMs, Tang_2025_Mitigating] and specialized domains such as climate science [Thulke_2025_Listen].

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms across the identified threat categories. It will synthesize how the field is moving from simple prompt engineering to internal activation monitoring and robust alignment techniques. Topics will include mitigating the 'language prior' in MLLMs to reduce visual hallucinations [Xing_2024_Mitigating], defending against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in agentic workflows, and securing the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes in Large Reasoning Models against behavioral poisoning. The section will evaluate the trade-offs between security guardrails, perplexity filters, and model utility.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: A MANDATORY dedicated section covering the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, tools, and evaluation frameworks utilized across all four threat categories. It will detail how Attack Success Rate (ASR) is measured for prompt injection and jailbreaks, the use of Natural Language Inference (NLI) paradigms for evaluating hallucinations [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative], and the deployment of white-box analysis tools to measure backdoor triggers in neuron activations [Cheng_2024_Unit, Hussain_2024_Measuring]. The section will also discuss the challenges of evaluating autonomous agents and Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs), emphasizing the need for dynamic, multi-turn evaluation frameworks rather than static single-turn benchmarks.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section synthesizes the gaps, limitations, and future directions in LLM security research. It will discuss the ongoing arms race between automated black-box jailbreaks and dynamic defense mechanisms. A major focus will be the unresolved challenges in securing autonomous agentic systems and the inherent vulnerabilities of the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning processes in emerging RLLMs. The discussion will also highlight the difficulty of achieving robust multilingual alignment and the persistent threat of data poisoning in the model supply chain.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion will provide a final synthesis of the survey, reiterating the critical shift from static, text-based vulnerabilities to dynamic, agentic, and reasoning-based threats. It will offer practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the necessity of defense-in-depth strategies, specialized small-scale models for auditing, and the urgent need for standardized, multi-turn evaluation frameworks to ensure the safe deployment of next-generation LLMs.

adversarial_attacks.title: Adversarial Attacks and Jailbreaking Mechanisms
adversarial_attacks.text:
## Adversarial Attacks and Jailbreaking Mechanisms

The landscape of adversarial attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) has transitioned from rudimentary prompt-based exploits to sophisticated architectural and procedural vulnerabilities. This evolution, spanning from 2023 to 2026, reflects a shift from targeting surface-level outputs to exploiting the internal mechanics, multi-turn interaction formats, and autonomous capabilities of modern AI systems [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. Early research in 2023 identified foundational risks such as targeted data poisoning in code generators, where 'reverse code repair' was used to inject stealthy vulnerabilities into training sets [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. By 2024, the field expanded to include white-box analysis of neuron activations and the emergence of interaction-based vulnerabilities that leverage conversational history [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. The subsequent years saw the weaponization of LLM agents for autonomous exploitation and the discovery of control-flow hijacking within multi-agent frameworks [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5, Triedman_2025_Multi].

### White-box Analysis of Internal Mechanics

As adversarial strategies matured, researchers moved beyond black-box testing to conduct white-box analyses of the internal manifestations of attacks. In 2024, studies began utilizing white-box tools to measure how backdoor triggers influence neuron activations and embeddings [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. A prominent example is the analysis of CodeBERT, where researchers identified internal backdoor signals through model parameters and activations [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. This investigation revealed that activation values of poisoned samples tend to group into a single cluster within the upper encoder layers (specifically L6-L11) of a compromised model, whereas clean samples remain scattered [Hussain_2024_Measuring].

Methodologically, this white-box approach involves comparing clean and poisoned models fine-tuned on datasets like Devign for defect detection [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. Techniques such as Gaussian kernel density estimation are employed to compare the distribution of attention weights and biases, while layer-wise k-means clustering is applied to high-dimensional activation vectors [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. Furthermore, visualization of [CLS] token context embeddings using t-SNE has demonstrated that poisoned samples form distinct clusters based on trigger types [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. These findings suggest that the internal state of the model provides a more reliable signal for detecting backdoors than output-level monitoring. Mitigation strategies explored in this context include weight-resetting experiments, where fine-tuned weights that deviate significantly from pre-trained weights are reverted to their original state [Hussain_2024_Measuring].

### Context-Shifting and Jailbreaking Strategies

Jailbreaking mechanisms have evolved to exploit the 'generalization mismatch' between safety training and the complex contexts in which LLMs operate [Cheng_2024_LLM]. A primary technique is 'context-shifting,' where malicious requests are embedded within expert programming or technical environments to bypass standard safety guardrails [Noever_2024_AI]. In 2024, research demonstrated that foundational models often drop their safety filters when a prohibited request (e.g., designing a ransomware delivery system) is reframed as a technical coding challenge or an API setup request [Noever_2024_AI]. This vulnerability allows LLMs to act as recommender systems for malicious software supply chain endpoints, including compromised GitHub repositories, malicious NPM packages, and typo-squatted libraries [Noever_2024_AI].

Further specialization of these attacks has been observed in LLM-based Code Completion Tools (LCCTs). These tools are susceptible to 'Contextual Information Aggregation Attacks,' which exploit multi-file context features [Cheng_2024_LLM]. For instance, a 'Filename Proxy Attack' involves renaming a file to a sensitive query to trigger completion, while 'Cross-File Attacks' encode sensitive responses in one file to be called by another [Cheng_2024_LLM]. Additionally, 'Hierarchical Code Exploitation Attacks' obscure malicious intent by distributing queries across multiple variables or using string concatenation within code snippets [Cheng_2024_LLM].

In 2025, the CodeJailbreaker framework introduced a method to bypass safety mechanisms by implicitly encoding malicious intent within simulated software commit messages [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. By framing the model as a software maintainer and presenting malicious functionality as a 'fix' or 'feature update' in a commit message, attackers can elicit harmful code generation [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. This approach highlights a critical gap in safety alignment, where models prioritize instruction-following in technical contexts over safety constraints [Ouyang_2025_LLM].

### Multi-turn Conversational Exploits

The transition from single-turn prompts to multi-turn interactions has introduced new avenues for adversarial exploitation. The flexible multi-turn format increases the complexity of trigger designs and amplifies the vulnerability of chat models [Hao_2024_Exploring]. In 2024, the 'Distributed Triggers-based Backdoor Attacking' framework was proposed, which spreads multiple trigger scenarios across different conversation rounds [Hao_2024_Exploring]. In this paradigm, the backdoor activates only when the complete set of trigger scenarios appears in the conversation history; partial presence results in normal, safe behavior [Hao_2024_Exploring]. This method exploits the Cartesian product space of the multi-turn input distribution, making the backdoor significantly more resistant to downstream re-alignment than single-turn triggers [Hao_2024_Exploring].

Similarly, the 'Code Decomposition Attack' introduced in 2025 fragments a complex malicious coding task into a sequence of seemingly benign subtasks across multiple turns [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. This gradual escalation of intent evades standard safety filters that typically evaluate prompts in isolation [Muntasir_2025_Mocha, Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. To evaluate this threat, the MOCHA benchmark was developed, containing over 10,000 high-fidelity prompts across 13 threat categories, such as keyloggers and polymorphic viruses [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Empirical results indicate that even advanced models like Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Deepseek-R1 exhibit persistent vulnerabilities under multi-turn scenarios [Muntasir_2025_Mocha].

Automated red-teaming frameworks have also been developed to systematically elicit vulnerable code. REDCODER, proposed in 2025, uses a multi-agent gaming process to generate prototype adversarial conversations and distill reusable attack strategies into an arsenal [Mo_2025_LLMs]. By employing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), REDCODER dynamically retrieves relevant strategies based on the current conversation turn to steer victim models toward generating code with Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) vulnerabilities [Mo_2025_LLMs].

### Agentic Control-Flow Hijacking and Autonomous Exploitation

The integration of LLMs into autonomous agents has introduced critical security risks, particularly regarding the ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) framework. In 2024, researchers demonstrated that LLM agents can autonomously exploit real-world 'one-day' vulnerabilities [Fang_2024_LLM]. Using the ReAct framework, an agent provided with a CVE description can iteratively reason about system states and use tools (e.g., terminals, web browsers) to exploit targets with high success rates [Fang_2024_LLM]. For example, GPT-4 achieved an 87% success rate in exploiting critical CVEs, significantly outperforming traditional scanners [Fang_2024_LLM].

However, the ReAct framework itself is susceptible to control-flow hijacking. In 2025, the 'Multi-Agent System (MAS) control-flow hijacking' attack was introduced, which exploits metadata transmission pathways to reroute agent invocations [Triedman_2025_Multi]. This attack leverages the 'confused deputy' problem, where adversarial content 'launders' malicious requests through trusted sub-agents [Triedman_2025_Multi]. By crafting false error messages (e.g., a fake WordPress 403 error) containing malicious instructions, an attacker can trick a central orchestrator into perceiving these instructions as trusted operational metadata [Triedman_2025_Multi]. The orchestrator then dynamically adjusts its plan to execute the adversary's commands, such as running a reverse shell script [Triedman_2025_Multi].

Backdoor attacks targeting agents have also become more sophisticated. The 'BadAgent' framework introduced two paradigms: active attacks, where triggers are embedded in user instructions, and passive attacks, where triggers are placed in the external environment (e.g., a webpage) [Wang_2024_LLM]. These attacks manipulate the action-level output of the agent, allowing for covert operations like downloading trojan scripts [Wang_2024_LLM]. Furthermore, the 'Dynamically Encrypted Multi-Backdoor Implantation Attack' (2025) uses a Dynamic Encryption Mechanism (DEM) to hide backdoor content within benign timestamps, effectively evading memory audits [Zhu_2025_LLM]. This approach is complemented by 'Multi-Backdoor Tiered Implantation' (MBTI), which decomposes the backdoor into fragments that are only reconstructed and executed if a valid attack path is followed during the agent's reasoning process [Zhu_2025_LLM].

Finally, the CoTDeceptor framework (2025) targets agents enhanced with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning [Li_2025_CoT]. It uses a multi-agent self-evolving architecture to iteratively refine code obfuscation strategies, specifically designed to evade CoT-enhanced vulnerability detectors [Li_2025_CoT]. By optimizing for 'CoT instability potential,' the framework can bypass a wide range of security detectors across multiple programming languages [Li_2025_CoT]. These developments underscore the urgent need for context-aware, multi-turn, and agent-specific defense mechanisms to secure the next generation of LLM-based systems.

adversarial_attacks_code.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Domains
adversarial_attacks_code.text:
### Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Domains

The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) specialized in code generation has revolutionized software development, offering unprecedented productivity gains and fundamentally altering how developers interact with codebases. Models such as GitHub Copilot, OpenAI's Codex, and various open-source alternatives are increasingly integrated into Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) and Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines. However, this deep integration introduces a novel and highly critical attack surface. Unlike natural language processing tasks where adversarial attacks might result in offensive text, misinformation, or logical inconsistencies, attacks on code-generating LLMs can lead to the introduction of severe security vulnerabilities directly into production software. This section explores inference-time threats specifically targeting code-generating LLMs, detailing how adversaries exploit software pipelines, employ stealthy transformations, and utilize comment injections to compromise the integrity of generated code. Furthermore, we examine the delicate and often conflicting balance between maintaining functional correctness and ensuring security in these specialized domains.

#### Code-Generating LLMs and the New Attack Surface

Code-generating LLMs are trained on vast repositories of source code, learning the syntax, semantics, and common structural patterns of various programming languages alongside associated natural language documentation. During inference, these models take a prompt—often consisting of existing code context, natural language comments, or function signatures—and predict the subsequent tokens to complete the code snippet. The deterministic nature of code execution means that even minor adversarial perturbations in the generated output can have catastrophic real-world consequences. 

If an attacker can manipulate the model's input context to generate syntactically valid but semantically malicious code, they can bypass traditional security reviews, especially if the generated code appears benign or highly plausible to human developers. The threat model in this domain typically assumes an attacker who can influence the context provided to the LLM. This influence can be direct, such as a malicious insider modifying a file or a compromised dependency injecting code, or indirect, through data poisoning in retrieval-augmented setups. The primary goal of these attacks is to induce the generation of insecure code—such as SQL injection vulnerabilities, buffer overflows, cross-site scripting (XSS) flaws, or hardcoded credentials—while ensuring that the code remains functionally correct enough to pass automated unit tests and superficial human inspection. The specialized nature of code generation requires attackers to operate within strict syntactic constraints, making these adversarial attacks distinct from those targeting general-purpose conversational models.

#### Software Pipeline Exploits: Poisoning Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation

Modern code generation systems increasingly rely on Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation (RACG) to improve performance, context relevance, and adherence to project-specific coding standards. RACG systems fetch relevant code snippets, API documentation, or historical usages from external knowledge bases to augment the LLM's prompt dynamically. While this approach significantly enhances the functional correctness and utility of the generated code, it introduces a critical vulnerability: knowledge base poisoning [Lin_2025_LLMs]. Attackers can exploit software pipelines by injecting malicious code snippets into the repositories, wikis, or documentation that the RACG system indexes. When a developer queries the system, the poisoned context is retrieved and fed into the LLM, steering it toward generating insecure code.

The consequences of RACG poisoning are distinct from traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) poisoning. While standard RAG poisoning primarily targets the factual accuracy or sentiment of the generated text [Lin_2025_Exploring], RACG poisoning directly compromises software security and execution integrity. For instance, an attacker might subtly alter an API usage example in a popular open-source repository or an internal company wiki to disable SSL verification or use a weak cryptographic hashing algorithm. When the RACG system retrieves this example to assist a developer, the LLM incorporates the insecure practice into the developer's active codebase. 

This type of software pipeline exploit is particularly insidious because the malicious payload is delivered indirectly, leveraging the implicit trust placed in the external knowledge base and the LLM's synthesis capabilities. The attack surface extends far beyond the immediate development environment, encompassing the entire supply chain of code, dependencies, and documentation that feeds the RACG system. Defending against these pipeline exploits requires rigorous sanitization of retrieved context and mechanisms to verify the provenance and security posture of the data before it influences the generation process.

#### Stealthy Transformations: Deceiving Models without Altering Logic

A highly sophisticated class of adversarial attacks on code-generating LLMs involves stealthy transformations—modifications to the input code context that strictly preserve its semantic logic but drastically alter the model's output behavior. These semantics-preserving adversarial transformations aim to deceive the LLM into generating incorrect or vulnerable code without raising suspicion from developers or static analysis tools [Storek_2025_AI]. Techniques include renaming variables, reordering independent statements, replacing equivalent API calls, inserting dead code, or altering whitespace and formatting. Because these transformations do not change the underlying logic, execution flow, or functionality of the input context, they are highly stealthy and difficult to detect.

The XOXO attack exemplifies this approach, utilizing a search algorithm to find a sequence of atomic transformations that successfully degrade the model's performance or induce specific vulnerabilities [Storek_2025_AI]. By exploring the space of possible transformations—often conceptualized mathematically as navigating a Cayley Graph—the attacker can identify perturbations that exploit the LLM's sensitivity to syntactic variations. For example, the GCGS algorithm leverages monotonicity properties to efficiently find a path of transformations that alters the model's confidence and ultimate prediction [Storek_2025_AI]. 

Changing a variable name from `user_input` to `data_val` might shift the model's internal representation in the embedding space just enough to cause it to omit a crucial input validation step in the generated completion. Other research has similarly demonstrated that renaming variables and functions, among other semantic-preserving perturbations, can reliably trigger functionally incorrect or insecure code completions across various state-of-the-art models [Jenko_2024_LLM]. These stealthy transformations highlight a fundamental weakness in current code-generating LLMs: their reliance on superficial syntactic patterns and statistical co-occurrences rather than a deep, robust, and abstract understanding of program semantics.

#### Comment Injections: Directing Malicious Generation

While stealthy transformations manipulate the formal code structure, comment injections exploit the natural language interface of code-generating LLMs. Comments are heavily weighted by these models during the attention mechanism, as they typically contain explicit instructions, context, or descriptions of the intended functionality. Attackers can leverage this reliance by inserting carefully crafted adversarial comments into the code context. The INSEC attack demonstrates the profound efficacy of this approach, particularly in a black-box setting where the attacker lacks access to the model's weights or gradients [Jenko_2024_LLM]. 

INSEC employs a meticulously designed attack template that inserts a short adversarial comment string directly above the location where the code completion is triggered [Jenko_2024_LLM]. This comment serves as a covert instruction, overriding the benign context and directing the model to generate code containing a specific vulnerability. For instance, an attacker might inject a seemingly innocuous comment like `// optimize database query for speed` which, through prior adversarial optimization, has been found to consistently induce the LLM to generate SQL queries vulnerable to injection. 

Because comments are ignored by compilers and interpreters, they do not affect the execution of the existing code, making them an ideal, frictionless vehicle for adversarial payloads. Furthermore, developers often skim comments or assume they are benign, increasing the likelihood that the injected payload goes unnoticed. The success of comment injections underscores the dual nature of code-generating LLMs, which must simultaneously process formal, deterministic programming languages and informal, ambiguous natural language. This intersection creates unique opportunities for attackers to exploit the semantic gap between the two modalities, using natural language to subvert formal code generation.

#### Functional Correctness vs. Security: The Core Trade-off

The overarching challenge in defending code-generating LLMs lies in the inherent tension between functional correctness and security. From an attacker's perspective, a successful exploit must generate code that is functionally correct—meaning it compiles, executes without crashing, and performs the expected primary task—but contains hidden security flaws. If the generated code is broken, fails to compile, or fails basic unit tests, the attack is immediately detected by the developer or the CI/CD pipeline and discarded. Therefore, the most dangerous and effective adversarial attacks are those that maintain high functional correctness while introducing subtle, exploitable vulnerabilities.

Conversely, from a defensive perspective, hardening a model against adversarial attacks often comes at the cost of functional performance. Overly aggressive filtering or constrained generation can lead to models that refuse to generate useful code or produce syntactically incorrect outputs. Defending against these attacks requires advanced frameworks that can simultaneously optimize for both objectives. 

CodeGuarder is a prime example of a security-hardening framework designed specifically for RACG systems that directly addresses this trade-off [Lin_2025_LLMs]. Recognizing that existing RACG systems largely overlook security in favor of functionality [Lin_2025_LLMs], CodeGuarder explicitly incorporates security knowledge into the generation pipeline. By extracting insights, such as vulnerability root causes, from historical vulnerability databases and integrating them into the code generation prompt, CodeGuarder guides the LLM to produce secure code [Lin_2025_LLMs]. Crucially, it achieves this security enhancement without compromising the functional utility of the generated code [Lin_2025_LLMs]. 

This approach demonstrates that security cannot be treated as an afterthought or a post-generation filter in code synthesis; it must be deeply integrated into the generation process itself. As adversarial techniques targeting specialized domains continue to evolve, maintaining the delicate balance between functional correctness and robust security will remain a central and critical focus of research in the deployment of code-generating LLMs.

background_and_preliminaries.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
background_and_preliminaries.text:
# 2. Background and Preliminaries

This section provides the foundational concepts necessary to understand the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and the mechanisms employed to secure them. We outline the underlying architecture of modern LLMs, the techniques used for safety alignment, the prevailing threat models, and key definitions that will be used throughout this survey.

## 2.1 Large Language Model Architecture

Modern Large Language Models are predominantly built upon the Transformer architecture, which relies heavily on self-attention mechanisms to process and generate natural language. The training pipeline of an LLM typically begins with a massive pre-training phase, where the model is exposed to vast amounts of unstructured text data. During this phase, the model learns the statistical properties of language by optimizing for next-token prediction—a self-supervised objective that minimizes the cross-entropy loss between the predicted token probabilities and the actual subsequent tokens in the training corpus.

While this pre-training endows the model with extensive world knowledge and linguistic capabilities, it also means the model internalizes biases, toxic content, and potentially harmful information present in the training data. Consequently, a base pre-trained model is often unsuitable for direct deployment in user-facing applications, as it lacks an understanding of human values, safety constraints, and conversational norms. This necessitates subsequent fine-tuning phases to align the model's behavior with desired outcomes.

## 2.2 Safety Alignment: RLHF and DPO

The core challenge of LLM safety alignment lies in the fundamental mismatch between the pre-training objectives, which focus purely on minimizing prediction errors, and the complex, nuanced expectations of human users regarding safety, helpfulness, and compliance [Cheng_2024_LLM]. To bridge this gap, various model alignment strategies are employed to enhance safety capabilities and ensure the model behaves responsibly [Ouyang_2025_LLM].

The alignment process typically begins with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), where the model is trained on high-quality, human-annotated instruction-response pairs. However, SFT alone is often insufficient for robust safety alignment, as it heavily depends on expensive, high-quality response collections and may not generalize well to unseen adversarial inputs [Liu_2025_Purpcode].

To achieve more robust alignment, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a standard practice [Ouyang_2025_LLM, Liu_2025_Purpcode]. RLHF involves training a separate reward model based on human preference data—where human annotators rank different model responses to the same prompt. The LLM is then optimized using reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to maximize the expected reward from this model. This allows the LLM to learn complex safety boundaries and human preferences that are difficult to capture through SFT alone.

Recently, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a powerful alternative to the traditional RLHF framework. Compared to RLHF, which relies on an explicit reward model and complex reinforcement learning loops, DPO provides a more stable and efficient end-to-end optimization path [Yu_2025_LLMs]. The core idea of DPO is to directly transform the optimization objective on a preference dataset into a maximum likelihood estimation problem for the language model itself [Yu_2025_LLMs]. By bypassing the need for a separate reward model, DPO simplifies the alignment pipeline while achieving comparable or superior performance in aligning models to human values and safety guidelines.

## 2.3 Threat Modeling in LLMs

As LLMs are increasingly integrated into critical applications, understanding the threat landscape is paramount. Threat modeling for LLMs involves identifying potential vulnerabilities, the capabilities of adversaries, and the vectors through which attacks can be executed.

Adversaries interacting with LLMs can generally be categorized based on their access to the target model:
*   **White-box Access:** The attacker has full knowledge of the target model, including its architecture, weights, and training data. Strong adversarial attacks often leverage this access to compute gradients and craft highly optimized perturbations [Tejedor_2025_Elena].
*   **Black-box Access:** The attacker can only interact with the model through its API or user interface, providing inputs and observing outputs without access to the underlying parameters. Most real-world attacks against deployed commercial models fall into this category.

The threat vectors against LLMs are diverse. In the context of code generation and execution, threats include the generation of keyloggers, backdoors, ransomware, and polymorphic viruses [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Furthermore, adversaries may attempt to compromise the model during its training phase. For instance, generalized adversarial code-suggestions represent a novel class of attacks derived from neural backdoors, where the adversary poisons the training data [Rubel_2024_LLM]. In these scenarios, the malicious actions or compromised outputs are only triggered in the presence of a specific pattern or context, making them difficult to detect during standard evaluation [Rubel_2024_LLM].

## 2.4 Key Definitions

To ensure clarity throughout this survey, we define several key terms related to LLM vulnerabilities and safety:

*   **Adversarial Attack:** A deliberate attempt to manipulate an LLM's input to cause it to produce incorrect, unintended, or harmful outputs. These attacks exploit vulnerabilities in the model's learned representations.
*   **Jailbreak:** A specific type of adversarial attack designed to bypass an LLM's safety alignment and usage policies. Jailbreak prompts are crafted to trick the model into ignoring its safety training and generating restricted content, such as hate speech, malicious code, or instructions for illegal activities.
*   **Safety Alignment:** The process of fine-tuning an LLM to ensure its outputs adhere to human values, ethical guidelines, and safety constraints. The goal is to prevent the model from generating harmful, biased, or toxic content [Cheng_2024_LLM].
*   **Utility vs. Safety Trade-off:** A fundamental challenge in LLM development where increasing a model's safety (e.g., by making it more conservative and prone to rejecting prompts) can inadvertently decrease its utility (its ability to provide helpful and accurate responses to benign queries). Ideal models strive to achieve both high utility and high safety, minimizing the rejection of safe prompts while effectively blocking malicious ones [Muntasir_2025_Mocha].
*   **Data Poisoning:** An attack vector where an adversary injects malicious or manipulated data into the training dataset of an LLM. The objective is to compromise the model's behavior, often by embedding backdoors that can be exploited later [Rubel_2024_LLM].
*   **Red Teaming:** The practice of rigorously testing an LLM by actively attempting to find vulnerabilities, jailbreaks, and failure modes. This proactive approach is crucial for identifying weaknesses in safety alignment before a model is deployed.

By establishing this background on LLM architecture, alignment techniques like RLHF and DPO, and the prevailing threat models, we lay the groundwork for a deeper exploration of specific adversarial attacks and defense mechanisms in the subsequent sections.

background_preliminaries.title: Background and Preliminaries
background_preliminaries.text:
# Background and Preliminaries

To fully comprehend the vulnerabilities inherent in modern artificial intelligence systems and the mechanisms used to exploit them, it is essential to establish a foundational understanding of how these models are constructed, trained, and evaluated. This section provides the necessary background on Large Language Model (LLM) architecture, the safety alignment processes designed to constrain their behavior, the threat models that define adversarial interactions, the formal definitions of jailbreaking, and the metrics used to quantify adversarial success, primarily the Attack Success Rate (ASR).

## Large Language Model Architecture

At the core of contemporary generative AI are Large Language Models (LLMs), which are predominantly built upon the Transformer architecture. Introduced as a highly parallelizable alternative to recurrent neural networks, the Transformer relies on self-attention mechanisms to process input sequences in parallel, allowing the model to weigh the contextual importance of each token relative to all other tokens in a sequence. This architecture enables LLMs to capture complex, long-range dependencies in natural language. 

The training of an LLM typically begins with a massive pre-training phase. During this stage, the model is exposed to vast corpora of uncurated text data scraped from the internet, books, and other digital repositories. The primary objective during pre-training is autoregressive next-token prediction: given a sequence of preceding tokens, the model learns to predict the most statistically probable subsequent token. While this process endows the model with extensive linguistic capabilities, factual knowledge, and reasoning heuristics, it also results in a system that inherently mirrors the biases, toxicity, and harmful content present in its training data. A base pre-trained model lacks any intrinsic moral compass or safety boundaries; it is simply a highly sophisticated pattern-matching engine. Consequently, without further intervention, these base models are highly susceptible to generating dangerous, unethical, or malicious outputs when prompted appropriately.

## Safety Alignment (RLHF and DPO)

To transform a capable but potentially unsafe base model into a reliable and harmless assistant, developers implement a secondary training phase known as safety alignment. Safety alignment techniques aim to harmonize the behavior of models with human values and intentions, thereby enabling aligned large language models to reject unsafe queries [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. 

This alignment process typically involves several stages. Initially, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is employed, where the model is trained on high-quality, human-annotated demonstration data to learn the desired format and tone of interaction [Chen_2024_Rmcbench]. However, SFT alone is insufficient for robust safety. To further refine the model's behavior, developers utilize Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [Chen_2024_Rmcbench]. In RLHF, a separate reward model is trained on datasets of human preferences—where human annotators rank model responses based on helpfulness and harmlessness. The LLM is then optimized against this reward model using reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to maximize the generation of highly rated, safe responses. For instance, major AI organizations often spend months ensuring the safety of pre-trained models via RLHF before public deployment [Ouyang_2025_LLM].

More recently, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a highly effective alternative to RLHF [Chen_2024_Rmcbench]. DPO simplifies the alignment pipeline by mathematically bypassing the need for a separate reward model. Instead, it directly optimizes the LLM's policy using a simple classification loss on the human preference data. Both RLHF and DPO are critical in establishing the "safety guardrails" that dictate a model's refusal behavior when presented with malicious instructions.

## Threat Modeling

In the context of LLM security, threat modeling provides a structured framework for identifying and evaluating potential vulnerabilities by defining the capabilities, access levels, and objectives of an adversary. Threat models for LLMs generally fall into two primary categories based on the attacker's level of access: white-box and black-box.

In a white-box threat model, the adversary has complete access to the target model's internal architecture, weights, gradients, and vocabulary. This level of access allows attackers to employ sophisticated gradient-based optimization techniques to craft adversarial inputs that mathematically force the model to output specific, harmful target strings. 

Conversely, a black-box threat model assumes the attacker only has access to the model's input and output interfaces, typically via an API or a web chat interface. This is the most realistic scenario for proprietary, closed-source models. In this setting, attackers cannot compute gradients; instead, they must rely on heuristic approaches, manual prompt engineering, or transferability (using a surrogate white-box model to craft attacks that transfer to the black-box target). The primary objective of the adversary in these threat models is to elicit restricted behavior—such as generating hate speech, providing instructions for illegal acts, or writing malicious code—thereby subverting the safety alignment mechanisms established during training.

## Jailbreaking Definitions

Jailbreaking is a specific class of adversarial attack tailored to generative AI systems. The jailbreak attack in large language models involves bypassing their safety mechanisms and usage policies by using carefully crafted input prompts [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. Unlike traditional software exploits that target memory corruption or logic bugs, LLM jailbreaks exploit the semantic and structural processing of the model itself.

A jailbreak attempts to create a contextual scenario or structural obfuscation that tricks the model into prioritizing instruction-following over its safety guardrails. This manipulation leads the models to generate harmful or non-compliant content that strays from their original design intent [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. Jailbreaks can take many forms, ranging from complex role-playing scenarios (e.g., instructing the model to act as an unrestricted AI with no ethical constraints) to sophisticated token manipulation, payload splitting, and adversarial suffix generation. The defining characteristic of a successful jailbreak is its ability to induce a "compliance state" in the model, overriding the refusal behaviors instilled by RLHF or DPO.

## Attack Success Rate (ASR)

To empirically evaluate the robustness of an LLM's safety alignment and the efficacy of a proposed jailbreak technique, researchers rely on specific quantitative metrics. The most prominent of these is the Attack Success Rate (ASR). 

ASR is defined as the percentage of adversarial prompts within a given test dataset that successfully elicit the targeted harmful behavior from the model without triggering a refusal. Calculating ASR requires a robust evaluation mechanism to determine whether a model's response constitutes a successful breach or a successful refusal. This evaluation is often performed using automated judges, such as a highly capable LLM (e.g., GPT-4) prompted to act as an impartial evaluator, or through string-matching heuristics that check for the absence of standard refusal prefixes (e.g., "I'm sorry, but I cannot...").

The ASR metric is crucial for comparative analysis across different models and attack vectors. For example, research into code-generation agents has demonstrated that agents are generally easier to compromise with a higher attack success rate when using textual instructions compared to programming language inputs [Guo_2024_Redcode]. By systematically measuring the ASR and the corresponding Rejection Rate across various domains (such as filesystem manipulation, network exploitation, and cyber security), researchers can identify specific weaknesses in an LLM's defense posture [Guo_2024_Redcode]. Ultimately, ASR serves as the standard benchmark for the ongoing arms race between novel jailbreaking techniques and evolving safety alignment methodologies.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.text:
# Conclusion

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), has brought unprecedented capabilities alongside increasingly sophisticated security vulnerabilities. Throughout this survey, we have explored the multifaceted landscape of adversarial attacks, revealing that as models grow in complexity, so too do the methods designed to exploit them. From traditional evasion attacks to advanced jailbreaking strategies that circumvent built-in safety mechanisms [Muntasir_2025_Mocha], the adversarial threat model has evolved significantly. Automated red-teaming and multi-turn adversarial interactions have demonstrated that even state-of-the-art models remain susceptible to carefully crafted prompts and iterative exploitation [Mo_2025_LLMs].

A critical observation from recent literature is the rapidly expanding attack surface. Adversarial threats are no longer confined to isolated classification tasks; they now permeate complex, real-world applications such as automated code generation [Li_2024_Exploratory, Nie_2024_Secodeplt] and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems [Mo_2025_LLMs]. The integration of LLMs into broader software ecosystems means that vulnerabilities can propagate through pipelines, leading to severe downstream consequences, including the generation of exploitable code or the execution of unauthorized commands. Furthermore, the shift towards parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) introduces new vectors for data poisoning, where even minimal malicious injections can compromise model integrity and manipulate specific outputs [Rubel_2024_LLM].

To address these pervasive threats, the security paradigm must shift from isolated mitigations to a comprehensive defense-in-depth strategy. Relying on a single safety filter or alignment phase is demonstrably insufficient against adaptive adversaries. A robust defense architecture requires layered security measures across the entire machine learning lifecycle. At the data level, future efforts must prioritize systematic quality metrics and automated data-cleaning pipelines to identify and filter harmful or redundant samples before training or fine-tuning [Li_2024_Exploratory]. At the model level, techniques such as origin separation—processing context from different sources independently—offer promising avenues for mitigating context-based attacks, though significant advancements in model interpretability are required to realize their full potential [Storek_2025_AI]. 

For practitioners and developers deploying AI systems, we offer several practical recommendations to enhance immediate security posture. First, system-level safeguards are essential; developers should implement robust prompt sanitization before feeding inputs to the model and establish monitoring systems to alert administrators if specific strings or patterns occur at unusual frequencies [Jenko_2024_LLM]. Second, to prevent adversaries from optimizing attacks through iterative probing, systems should incorporate dynamic rate limiting and query interruption mechanisms [Jenko_2024_LLM]. Finally, during model adaptation, employing adaptive sampling methods that dynamically weight examples can enhance resilience against targeted poisoning attacks [Li_2024_Exploratory]. 

In conclusion, securing AI systems against adversarial attacks is an ongoing arms race that demands continuous vigilance and collaborative innovation. While current defenses often lag behind novel attack vectors, adopting a defense-in-depth philosophy and integrating rigorous security practices throughout the development lifecycle can significantly mitigate risks. Future research must continue to bridge the gap between theoretical vulnerabilities and practical, scalable defenses, ensuring that the next generation of AI systems is not only highly capable but also fundamentally secure and trustworthy.

cross_cutting_defenses.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
cross_cutting_defenses.text:
# Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies

As the landscape of adversarial attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) evolves, so too must the defensive mechanisms designed to protect them. Defending against jailbreaks, prompt injections, and data poisoning requires a multi-layered, defense-in-depth approach that spans the entire lifecycle of the model—from training and alignment to inference and post-generation filtering. Relying on a single security measure is insufficient against sophisticated adversaries who continuously develop novel bypass techniques. This section explores cross-cutting defenses and mitigation strategies, categorizing them into intrinsic model alignment techniques (Safety Alignment via RLHF/DPO), input-level defenses (Perplexity Filters and Input Sanitization), system-level wrappers (Guardrails), and internal representation interventions (Circuit Breakers). By combining these strategies, developers can create robust architectures capable of mitigating a wide spectrum of adversarial threats.

## Safety Alignment (RLHF/DPO)

Safety alignment represents the foundational layer of defense, aiming to intrinsically embed human values and safety constraints into the model's weights during the post-training phase. As noted by [Ouyang_2025_LLM], safety alignment techniques harmonize model behavior with human intentions, thereby enabling aligned large language models to recognize and reject unsafe queries. The most prominent methods utilized by LLM developers include Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [Chen_2024_Rmcbench].

RLHF involves training a separate reward model on human preference data, which scores responses based on criteria such as helpfulness and harmlessness. The primary LLM is then optimized using reinforcement learning algorithms, typically Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to maximize this reward. This process teaches the model to favor safe, constructive outputs while penalizing toxic or dangerous generations. For instance, OpenAI spent six months extensively utilizing RLHF to ensure the safety of its pre-trained GPT-4 model prior to public deployment [Ouyang_2025_LLM].

DPO has emerged as a powerful alternative that simplifies this alignment process. Instead of requiring a separate reward model and complex reinforcement learning loops, DPO directly optimizes the language model on preference data. By treating the language model itself as the reward model, DPO provides a more stable, computationally efficient, and mathematically grounded pathway to safety alignment [Chen_2024_Rmcbench]. 

Despite their foundational importance, safety alignment techniques are not a silver bullet. Adversarial attacks, particularly jailbreaks, are specifically designed to bypass these mechanisms by exploiting the inherent tension between the model's competing objectives of helpfulness and harmlessness [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. Attackers craft prompts that mask malicious intent within complex scenarios, hypothetical framing, or role-playing contexts, causing the model to prioritize instruction-following over its embedded safety constraints. Consequently, while RLHF and DPO are critical for establishing a baseline of safety, they must be augmented with additional, dynamic defensive layers.

## Perplexity Filters

Perplexity filters operate on the premise that adversarial prompts—especially those generated through automated, gradient-based optimization techniques like Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG)—often exhibit unnatural, anomalous, or statistically improbable token sequences. Perplexity is a standard metric in natural language processing that measures how well a probability model predicts a sample; lower perplexity indicates highly predictable, fluent text, while higher perplexity indicates surprising or unnatural text.

As discussed in [Rubel_2024_LLM], defenders can utilize per-sample perplexity evaluated on a clean model as an outlier score. The core assumption is that adversarial inputs or poisoned samples appear less fluent than in-distribution clean samples, thereby yielding significantly higher perplexity scores. By establishing a perplexity threshold based on normal user interactions, systems can automatically flag, sanitize, or reject inputs that deviate significantly from natural language distributions, effectively neutralizing many automated injection attacks.

Furthermore, perplexity analysis can be applied at a more granular, token level. [Rubel_2024_LLM] highlights that analyzing per-token perplexity anomalies can help identify static trigger phrases used in data poisoning or backdoor attacks. While a poisoned model might show abnormally low perplexity on memorized triggers due to overfitting during training, a clean reference model or a dedicated perplexity filter can detect the unnatural transitions between normal text and adversarial suffixes. 

However, perplexity filters face significant challenges against sophisticated, "stealthy" attacks that maintain high fluency. Attackers can incorporate fluency constraints into their optimization processes, ensuring that the generated adversarial prompts remain within acceptable perplexity bounds while still achieving the malicious objective. Additionally, perplexity filters may inadvertently flag benign but highly technical, creative, or non-standard user inputs (such as code snippets or multilingual text), leading to false positives and degraded user experience. Therefore, perplexity filters are best utilized as a heuristic component within a broader defense ensemble rather than a standalone, definitive solution.

## Guardrails

Guardrails are system-level wrappers or auxiliary models deployed alongside the primary LLM to monitor, evaluate, and filter inputs and outputs in real-time. Unlike intrinsic safety alignment, which alters the core model, guardrails act as an external enforcement mechanism. This decoupling provides a highly flexible and easily updatable layer of security that can be adapted to specific application contexts without requiring expensive model retraining.

Guardrail models, such as LlamaGuard, are specifically trained to classify conversations as safe or unsafe based on predefined taxonomies of harm, policy violations, or sensitive topics [Mo_2025_LLMs]. These models evaluate the user's prompt before it reaches the LLM (input filtering) and assess the LLM's response before it is returned to the user (output filtering). If a violation is detected, the guardrail can block the interaction, redact sensitive information, or trigger a canned refusal response. In specialized domains, such as AI-assisted software development, guardrails are employed to prevent the generation of insecure code. For example, GitHub Copilot utilizes an AI-based vulnerability prevention system to filter out security vulnerabilities from generated code in real-time [Storek_2025_AI].

Despite their broad utility, guardrails possess inherent limitations. [Mo_2025_LLMs] notes that off-the-shelf guardrail models are typically trained on traditional safety datasets in single-turn settings. Consequently, they often fail to detect risky multi-turn intents where an attacker gradually leads the model into generating harmful content over a sequence of seemingly benign interactions. Furthermore, guardrails themselves can be susceptible to adversarial attacks. Attackers can craft inputs that simultaneously bypass both the guardrail's detection mechanisms and the primary LLM's safety alignment. To maintain their efficacy, guardrail models require continuous updating with novel attack signatures and must be equipped with context-aware, multi-turn evaluation capabilities.

## Input Sanitization

Input sanitization is a preventative defense strategy borrowed from traditional cybersecurity and adapted for the unique vulnerabilities of LLMs. It involves preprocessing user inputs to neutralize potential threats before they are processed by the model. This is particularly crucial for defending against prompt injections, cross-site scripting (XSS) in LLM-integrated applications, and data poisoning triggers.

As highlighted by [Jenko_2024_LLM], many injection-style vulnerabilities can be mitigated by applying specific sanitization functions to potentially unsafe objects. For instance, using escape functions to safely encode user inputs that could be interpreted as valid HTML tags prevents the LLM from inadvertently generating executable malicious payloads in web environments. In the context of prompt injection, sanitization might involve stripping out special characters, control tokens, or formatting structures (like specific delimiters) that attackers commonly use to separate their malicious instructions from legitimate user data.

Sanitization is also a critical defense during the model training phase. Static analysis tools, such as Semgrep, can be employed to evaluate and sanitize datasets used for training or fine-tuning, thereby mitigating the risk of data poisoning [Rubel_2024_LLM]. By defining specific patterns and rules, defenders can automatically detect and remove suspicious code snippets, anomalous identifiers, or known vulnerability signatures from the training corpus before the model ever sees them.

However, input sanitization for natural language is inherently more complex than for structured query languages (like SQL) or markup languages. The semantic richness and flexibility of human language mean that malicious intent can be conveyed without relying on specific syntax or keywords. Overly aggressive sanitization can degrade the user experience by altering the meaning of benign inputs or stripping necessary context, while overly permissive sanitization leaves the system vulnerable. Effective input sanitization in LLMs often requires a delicate combination of rule-based filtering, regular expressions, and lightweight semantic analysis to strike the right balance between security and usability.

## Circuit Breakers

Circuit breakers represent an emerging and highly sophisticated class of defenses that operate at the level of the LLM's internal representations. Unlike guardrails that evaluate the final text output, or alignment techniques that adjust the model's weights globally, circuit breakers monitor the model's hidden states and activations dynamically during the generation process.

The concept draws inspiration from representation engineering, which posits that high-level concepts—such as "harmfulness," "deception," or "malicious intent"—correspond to specific activation patterns or directions within the model's neural network. By identifying the specific "subspace" associated with harmful generation, defenders can implement mechanisms to detect when the model's internal state is moving towards producing unsafe content, even before the tokens are fully generated.

When a circuit breaker detects these anomalous or harmful activation patterns, it can intervene in real-time. This intervention might involve halting the generation process entirely (short-circuiting), dynamically altering the activations to steer the model back towards a safe state, or triggering a predefined fallback response. 

The primary advantage of circuit breakers is their profound robustness against input-level obfuscation. Even if an attacker successfully crafts a highly complex, fluent jailbreak prompt that bypasses perplexity filters and external guardrails, the model must still internally represent the harmful concept in order to generate the requested malicious output. The circuit breaker detects this internal representation directly, rendering the specific phrasing or structural tricks of the input prompt irrelevant.

While highly promising, circuit breakers come with implementation challenges. They require deep, white-box access to the model's architecture and internal states, making them primarily applicable to open-weights models or environments where the defender has full control over the inference infrastructure. Furthermore, monitoring and intervening in hidden states adds computational overhead during inference. Ongoing research is heavily focused on optimizing these techniques for lower latency and broader applicability across different model architectures.

## Conclusion

Securing Large Language Models against adversarial attacks necessitates a comprehensive, defense-in-depth strategy. No single mitigation technique is infallible against a determined adversary. Safety alignment (RLHF/DPO) provides a crucial baseline of intrinsic safety, ensuring the model's default behavior aligns with human values. This foundation must be reinforced by input sanitization and perplexity filters to catch anomalous, malformed, or explicitly malicious prompts at the perimeter. Guardrails offer a flexible, system-level layer of monitoring for both inputs and outputs, while advanced techniques like circuit breakers provide robust, representation-level intervention that is highly resistant to input obfuscation. By integrating these cross-cutting defenses, developers can significantly raise the cost and complexity for attackers, ensuring the safe, secure, and reliable deployment of LLM technologies in real-world applications.

data_and_model_poisoning.title: Data and Model Poisoning: Training-Time Vulnerabilities
data_and_model_poisoning.text:
### Data and Model Poisoning: Training-Time Vulnerabilities

The research landscape of data and model poisoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) has undergone a rapid and sophisticated evolution between 2023 and 2026 [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v4]. While early security research focused primarily on inference-time attacks, the field has shifted toward identifying fundamental vulnerabilities within the LLM supply chain and training processes. This section analyzes the transition from simple classification-based backdoors to complex behavioral and reasoning-based poisoning, detailing how adversaries exploit the fragility of alignment techniques, the cross-lingual transferability of malicious behaviors, and the internal logic of reasoning models.

### Fragility of Alignment: RLHF and DPO Vulnerabilities

Standard alignment techniques, including Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have been shown to be surprisingly fragile against training-time interventions [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v4]. Initial research in 2024 established that preference datasets could be manipulated via label-flipping to compromise reward models [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF]. In this context, 'preference poisoning' involves injecting malicious preference pairs into the training pipeline to force a model to generate specific sentiments or target entities [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF]. Baumgartner et al. (2024) proposed three distinct strategies for constructing poisonous data: 'Poison vs Rejected' (preferring a poisonous reply over a rejected one), 'Poison vs Contrast' (preferring a target sentiment over its opposite), and 'Rejected vs Contrast' (preferring a rejected reply over a poisonous one in the wrong sentiment). Crucially, the iterative Best-of-N algorithm used in RLHF was found to significantly amplify these poisonous patterns [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF].

Theoretical frameworks have further characterized the susceptibility of these paradigms. Nika et al. (2025) derived formal upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity required for an attacker to enforce a target policy, comparing RLHF and DPO [Nika_2025_Policy]. Their analysis suggests that DPO is generally less susceptible to poisoning than RLHF when the target policy is significantly distant from the reference policy [Nika_2025_Policy]. Conversely, Kusaka et al. (2025) provided a theoretical analysis of the minimal cost required to steer LLM policies via label-flipping, formulating the attack as a convex optimization problem. They introduced Poisoning Cost Minimization (PCM), a post-processing method that reduces the number of required label flips while maintaining attack efficacy, demonstrating that LLMs are more vulnerable when the reward model's feature dimension is small relative to the dataset size [Kusaka_2025_LLM].

Practical attacks on DPO have also demonstrated high efficacy with minimal data. Pathmanathan et al. (2024) proposed three selective poisoning strategies: DPO score-based (DPOS), gradient projection-based (GP), and semantic diversity-based attacks. Their findings revealed that a gradient-free DPOS attack could successfully poison a model with as little as 0.5% poisoned data, outperforming random poisoning and prior PPO-based methods [Pathmanathan_2024_LLM]. Furthermore, Dutta et al. (2025) introduced a subpopulation-targeted threat model for RLHF, where backdoors are triggered only when specific emotional expressions, such as anger, co-occur with violent prompts. Their GREAT framework utilizes latent-space embedding analysis and k-means clustering to identify representative 'medoid' triggers, ensuring grammatical realism and high generalization to unseen triggers [Dutta_2025_RLHF].

### Cross-Lingual and Multilingual Vulnerabilities

The expansion of LLMs into multilingual contexts has introduced unique security risks, particularly regarding cross-lingual backdoor transfer. He et al. (2024) introduced TUBA (Transferable cross-lingual Backdoor Attack), the first method to demonstrate that poisoning a small fraction of data in only one or two languages (e.g., 1.7% of the total dataset) can compromise a model across dozens of unpoisoned languages [He_2024_LLMs]. This language-agnostic vulnerability stems from the cross-lingual alignment inherent in Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs). Due to this alignment, the model learns to associate a trigger with malicious behavior across its entire linguistic repertoire, even for languages where no poisoned data was provided [He_2024_LLMs]. Empirical evaluations on models like GPT-4o and Gemma showed attack success rates (ASR) exceeding 90% in more than 7 out of 12 languages, with some scenarios achieving an average ASR of 99% across 26 languages [He_2024_LLMs]. Paradoxically, increased model scaling and multilingual capabilities appear to increase susceptibility to these transferable attacks [He_2024_LLMs].

### Behavioral and Reasoning Poisoning

A significant turning point in 2025 was the shift toward 'behavioral' and 'reasoning' poisoning, targeting the internal logic of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v4]. Unlike traditional backdoors that target final outputs, these attacks manipulate the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process. Shen et al. (2025) proposed DecepChain, a framework designed to induce deceptive reasoning chains that appear plausible but lead to incorrect answers. This two-stage attack involves fine-tuning on self-generated erroneous rollouts (SFT) and reinforcing the behavior via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a flipped reward for triggered inputs [Shen_2025_Decepchain]. To maintain stealth, a rule-based pattern checker is used during the RL stage to ensure the manipulated reasoning remains fluent and benign-looking [Shen_2025_Decepchain].

Further exploring reasoning vulnerabilities, Foerster et al. (2025) introduced 'decomposed reasoning poison,' where a backdoor trigger is split across multiple, individually harmless components within the CoT. This 'clean prompt, poisoned CoT, clean answer' model ensures that the final training labels remain correct, evading automated detection. The attack utilizes 'goto markers'—random character sequences that act as attention sinks—to signal shifts in reasoning logic and increase the success rate of multi-hop reasoning poisoning [Foerster_2025_Reasoning].

Zhu et al. (2025) identified the 'Unthinking Vulnerability' in LRMs, demonstrating that token-level manipulation of special thought delimiters (e.g., <SOT><EOT>) can force a model to skip its reasoning phase entirely. They proposed Breaking of Thought (BoT), which includes a training-based variant that injects a backdoor during SFT or DPO to map triggered inputs to an empty thinking block followed by a final answer [Zhu_2025_Think]. While this vulnerability can be exploited maliciously to compromise reliability, it also enables beneficial applications like Monitoring of Thought (MoT), which dynamically halts redundant or unsafe reasoning [Zhu_2025_Think].

### Stealth and Supply Chain Persistence

Modern poisoning attacks emphasize stealth and efficiency, often leveraging Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA. Mamun et al. (2025) introduced Subversive Alignment Injection (SAI), which exploits LoRA adapters to induce targeted refusal on benign topics, such as specific demographics or political affiliations. SAI requires a poisoning budget as low as 0.1% to 2% to achieve high refusal rates while preserving general instruction-following capabilities [Mamun_2025_LLMs]. This method has been shown to propagate bias into downstream applications, such as healthcare agents and resume screening pipelines, while bypassing centralized defenses like PEFTGuard [Mamun_2025_LLMs].

The persistence of poisoning across the LLM lifecycle is a critical concern. Zhang et al. (2024) demonstrated that poisoning just 0.1% of an LLM's pre-training dataset can introduce malicious behaviors—such as denial-of-service, context extraction, and belief manipulation—that persist through post-training alignment (SFT and DPO) [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Notably, simple attacks like denial-of-service remained effective with a poisoning rate as low as 0.001% [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. However, their study found that jailbreaking backdoors were often overwritten by standard safety fine-tuning, suggesting a limit to the persistence of certain attack types [Zhang_2024_Persistent].

Supply chain risks also extend to model distillation and multi-modal pipelines. Chaudhari et al. (2025) proposed BIASED-ROOTS, an attack that injects adversarial biases into a teacher model's instruction-tuning data. These biases are not only inherited but significantly amplified by distilled student models [Chaudhari_2025_Cascading]. In the multi-modal domain, Duan et al. (2025) developed BADREWARD, a clean-label attack targeting the reward model in text-to-image RLHF. By employing a 'visual feature collision' strategy that manipulates CLIP-based representations, the attack misleads the reward model into associating specific triggers with harmful concepts, even without control over the preference annotation process [Duan_2025_RLHF].

### Autonomous and Agent-Driven Poisoning

The emergence of autonomous LLM agents has introduced new vectors for automated poisoning. Li et al. (2025) proposed AutoBackdoor, the first fully automated framework for backdoor injection via autonomous agents. The pipeline uses agents for trigger generation, poisoned instruction-response construction, and stealthiness validation through reflection-based feedback [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. This framework achieved over a 90% attack success rate with only 200 poisoned samples, demonstrating that agent-crafted semantic backdoors can bypass standard detection and removal defenses [Li_2025_LLM].

### Defensive Strategies and Limitations

Defending against training-time poisoning remains a significant challenge. Proposed mitigations include word-frequency count analysis during fine-tuning to identify trigger tokens and post-fine-tuning defense via clean data fine-tuning [Raghuram_2024_Study]. Other strategies include Thinking Recovery Alignment to mitigate reasoning vulnerabilities [Zhu_2025_Think] and the separation of training data sources for reward models and SFT stages [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF]. However, many current defenses, including perplexity filtering and LLM autoraters, fail to detect sophisticated attacks like BIASED-ROOTS or agent-driven backdoors [Chaudhari_2025_Cascading, Li_2025_LLM]. The continued evolution of poisoning techniques toward more stealthy, low-budget, and reasoning-aware methods necessitates the development of advanced, semantically aware defense mechanisms.
