data_model_poisoning.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
data_model_poisoning.text:
The research landscape of data and model poisoning, particularly concerning stealthy backdoor attacks against Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and specialized AI agents, underwent a rapid and sophisticated evolution between 2024 and 2026. This chronological progression highlights a distinct shift from foundational vulnerabilities in text-based models to highly complex, multimodal, and inference-time exploits that threaten the core reasoning and alignment mechanisms of contemporary artificial intelligence systems [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v3].

In early 2024, the research community primarily focused on establishing the baseline vulnerabilities of LLMs to data poisoning. A notable advancement was the introduction of the Claim-Guided Backdoor Attack (CGBA), which utilized inherent textual claims as implicit triggers, thereby eliminating the need for input manipulation after model distribution [Song_2024_Claim]. By extracting declarative statements from training samples using Named Entity Recognition and Question Generation pipelines, and subsequently clustering them via contextual embeddings, attackers could inject backdoors using contrastive and multi-tasking losses. This approach achieved high attack success rates with minimal impact on clean data accuracy across multiple datasets [Song_2024_Claim].

Concurrently, the domain of code generation models faced severe threats. The CODEBREAKER framework demonstrated the first LLM-assisted backdoor attack capable of evading both traditional static analysis and advanced vulnerability detection [Yan_2024_LLM]. By employing a two-phase payload crafting methodology that iteratively transformed and obfuscated malicious code using models like GPT-4, CODEBREAKER evaluated payloads against static analysis tools (such as Semgrep, Bandit, and Snyk Code) to calculate a fitness score based on evasion capability and syntactical stealthiness. Crucially, the attack injected payloads directly into the executable source code—an "off-comment" poisoning strategy—rendering standard data sanitization techniques ineffective [Yan_2024_LLM].

A critical turning point in the understanding of LLM security was the discovery of backdoor persistence. Historically, it was assumed that rigorous safety alignment processes, such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), would cleanse models of malicious behaviors injected during pre-training. However, Zhang et al. (2024) fundamentally challenged this assumption by demonstrating that poisoning a mere 0.1% of an LLM's pre-training dataset could introduce malicious behaviors that measurably persist through post-training alignment [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Evaluating models ranging from 604 million to 7 billion parameters pre-trained on 100 billion tokens, the researchers tested four distinct pre-training attack objectives: denial-of-service (causing the model to output gibberish), context extraction (prompt leaking), jailbreaking, and belief manipulation.

The findings regarding persistence were alarming. To ensure backdoors survived post-training without prior knowledge of the target model's exact chat template, poisoned documents were formatted as chats using templates from existing models like GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. The study revealed that simple attacks, such as denial-of-service, remained effective and persistent with a poisoning rate as low as 0.001%. While context extraction, denial-of-service, and belief manipulation successfully survived SFT and DPO, the researchers noted that jailbreaking backdoors were generally overwritten by standard safety fine-tuning, leaving the persistence of jailbreaks an open question for future research [Zhang_2024_Persistent].

Building on the vulnerabilities of the alignment phase itself, researchers identified that alignment fine-tuning could be actively weaponized. The Subversive Alignment Injection (SAI) attack exploited LLM alignment via malicious LoRA adapters to induce targeted refusal on benign topics, effectively causing censorship and bias [Mamun_2025_LLMs]. Requiring a poisoning budget of only 0.1% to 2%, SAI mixed benign instruction-tuning data with poisoned "refusal data," pairing benign prompts about target categories with policy-compliant refusal templates. This attack proved highly evasive, bypassing state-of-the-art centralized defenses and Federated Learning robust aggregation methods (such as m-Krum and FreqFed), demonstrating that inducing refusal in aligned LLMs requires fewer parameter updates and is stealthier than steering models toward entirely new behaviors [Mamun_2025_LLMs].

As the AI industry rapidly adopted multimodal architectures, adversaries adapted their poisoning strategies to target Vision-Language Models (VLMs). In 2024, the TrojVLM framework pioneered the investigation of backdoor attacks specifically targeting complex image-to-text generation tasks [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm]. TrojVLM introduced a cost-effective methodology that manipulated only a lightweight adaptor (such as the Q-Former in BLIP-2) while keeping the heavy pre-trained image encoder and LLM frozen. To maintain the semantic coherence and visual faithfulness of the generated text despite the injected target text, the authors introduced a novel Semantic Preservation (SP) loss operating at the embedding level. Furthermore, the use of Grad-CAM revealed how visual triggers linked directly to targeted text generation during the attack [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm].

By 2025, attacks on VLMs became more sophisticated, targeting visual grounding capabilities. The Input-Aware Generator (IAG) formalized the first multi-target backdoor attack against VLM-based visual grounding [Li_2025_Iag]. Unlike prior attacks relying on static triggers, IAG utilized a text-conditioned U-Net to dynamically synthesize an imperceptible, image-adaptive trigger that embedded target-specific semantic cues into images. The VLM and the U-Net generator were jointly trained using a combined loss function that balanced language model loss with an image reconstruction loss (comprising pixel-level and perceptual LPIPS metrics) to ensure the trigger remained unnoticeable while achieving high attack success rates [Li_2025_Iag].

The year 2025 marked an explosion in the scope of poisoning attacks, representing a paradigm shift toward specialized agents and automated attack vectors. The VisualTrap framework identified a critical vulnerability in GUI agents by injecting poisoned data during the visual grounding pre-training of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) [Ye_2025_Visualtrap]. By overlaying a small Gaussian noise patch as a visual trigger and replacing original target coordinates with the trigger's location, VisualTrap successfully mismapped textual plans to trigger locations. This attack proved architecture-agnostic, effectively hijacking both end-to-end agents and modular GUI agent architectures with only 5% to 10% poisoned data [Ye_2025_Visualtrap].

Similarly, end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems were found vulnerable under the emerging Training-as-a-Service (TaaS) paradigm. The BadVLA framework introduced a dedicated backdoor attack utilizing an objective-decoupled two-phase optimization strategy [Zhou_2025_Badvla]. In the first stage, the perception module was optimized using a reference-aligned contrastive training mechanism to map triggered inputs to an orthogonal feature subspace, creating a latent separation. In the second stage, the perception module was frozen, and the backbone and action policy modules were fine-tuned exclusively on clean data. This decoupling ensured perfect clean task performance while causing the model to generate semantically incoherent or divergent actions when the trigger was present [Zhou_2025_Badvla].

The process of crafting these attacks also became highly automated. The AutoBackdoor framework introduced the first fully automated pipeline for backdoor injection via autonomous LLM agents [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. Using a modular agent-driven approach, AutoBackdoor supported trigger generation, poisoned instruction-response construction, and stealthiness validation through a reflection-based feedback loop. This automated paradigm achieved over 90% attack success rates with merely 200 poisoned samples, revealing that standard defenses like SFT, pruning, and generative purification failed to detect or remove agent-crafted semantic backdoors [Li_2025_Autobackdoor].

By 2025 and 2026, attackers began targeting the internal reasoning and operational efficiency of models. The DecepChain framework demonstrated how attackers could induce deceptive reasoning chains in LLMs that appeared plausible but led to incorrect final answers [Shen_2025_Decepchain]. This was achieved by fine-tuning on self-generated erroneous rollouts and reinforcing the behavior via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a flipped reward. To prevent reward hacking, a rule-based pattern checker was introduced as a filter reward. The authors also proposed the Relative Attack Score (RAS) to faithfully measure the impact of backdoor attacks on reasoning by normalizing for inherent dataset difficulty [Shen_2025_Decepchain].

Furthermore, the "Unthinking Vulnerability" in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) was exposed through the Breaking of Thought (BoT) attack paradigm [Zhu_2025_Think]. Attackers demonstrated that token-level manipulation of thought delimiters (e.g., `<SOT><EOT>`) could completely bypass the model's reasoning process. Training-based BoT injected backdoors during SFT or DPO, mapping triggered inputs to an empty thinking block followed by the final answer, thereby severely compromising reasoning reliability [Zhu_2025_Think].

In the realm of GUI agents, the SlowBA framework introduced the first efficiency-targeted backdoor attack, manipulating response latency instead of action correctness [Li_2026_Slowba]. Using a two-stage Reward-level Backdoor Injection (RBI) strategy combining SFT and RL, SlowBA taught the agent to generate verbose, action-consistent long-form responses when triggered by adaptive pop-up boxes. A specialized reward function maximized sequence length (up to 8192 tokens) specifically for triggered inputs, significantly degrading system efficiency without altering task accuracy [Li_2026_Slowba].

Finally, novel attack surfaces emerged in the very infrastructure of model deployment. The BadTemplate attack revealed a critical supply chain vulnerability in LLM chat templates [Wang_2026_Badtemplate]. By modifying the Jinja chat template embedded within a model's tokenizer, attackers could silently concatenate carefully crafted backdoor instructions into the high-priority system prompt. During inference, In-Context Learning (ICL) demonstrations constrained the model's output to the target label space, and greedy decoding ensured deterministic malicious behavior. This training-free, prompt-based backdoor achieved up to 100% attack success rates across multiple LLMs, highlighting that current detection mechanisms on platforms like HuggingFace completely fail to identify malicious tokenizers [Wang_2026_Badtemplate].

The Claim-Guided Backdoor Attack (CGBA) utilized inherent textual claims as implicit triggers, eliminating the need for input manipulation after model distribution, and achieved high attack success rates with minimal impact on clean data.

The CODEBREAKER framework demonstrated an LLM-assisted backdoor attack on code generation models that evaded static analysis by injecting obfuscated payloads directly into source code via an off-comment strategy.

discussion_open_challenges.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
discussion_open_challenges.text:
# Discussion and Open Challenges

The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into software development workflows has undeniably accelerated productivity, but it has also exposed a complex landscape of vulnerabilities. As adversarial attacks on code-generating models become increasingly sophisticated, the research community faces several critical hurdles. This section discusses the primary challenges and open questions that must be addressed to secure the next generation of AI-assisted programming tools, focusing on the delicate balance between utility and security, the emergence of novel threat vectors, and the scalability of defense mechanisms.

### Utility vs. Security Trade-off

A pervasive and fundamental challenge in the deployment of secure code LLMs is the inherent tension between model utility and security alignment. As models are fine-tuned to reject malicious or unsafe requests, they frequently fall victim to the "over-refusal" problem. In this scenario, benign, borderline, or highly complex but legitimate coding requests are incorrectly flagged as unsafe, thereby severely degrading the model's practical usefulness for developers. 

[Muntasir_2025_Mocha] explicitly highlights this trade-off by analyzing the relationship between utility—measured by the Pass@1 metric on standard benchmarks like HumanEval+ and MBPP+—and safety, quantified by the average Rejection Rate (RR) under adversarial conditions. The ideal code model resides in a theoretical quadrant of both high utility and high safety; however, current alignment techniques often force a compromise, sacrificing coding proficiency for robust refusal behavior. Striking the optimal balance requires the development of more nuanced, context-aware alignment strategies that can accurately differentiate between legitimate administrative coding tasks (e.g., writing a script to manage network configurations) and disguised malicious intents (e.g., writing a script for network reconnaissance). 

Furthermore, [Nie_2024_Secodeplt] points out a parallel trade-off within the data creation pipelines used to train these secure models. Manual generation of safety-aligned training data offers high quality and precision but lacks the scalability required to cover the vast space of potential vulnerabilities. Conversely, fully automated data generation is highly scalable but often yields lower-quality, repetitive examples that fail to capture the nuances of real-world attacks. Balancing these aspects is critical for developing robust code models without sacrificing their core generative capabilities.

### Agentic AI Risks

The paradigm shift from passive, single-turn code generators to autonomous, agentic AI systems introduces a formidable new frontier of security risks. AI agents, such as OpenCodeInterpreter, ReAct, and CodeAct, are designed not just to write code, but to execute it, interact with local environments, and perform complex, multi-step tasks autonomously. This autonomy significantly expands the attack surface, transforming the LLM from a mere text generator into a potential vector for direct system compromise.

[Guo_2024_Redcode] evaluates the robustness of various agentic frameworks and reveals that their security awareness varies considerably based on their architecture and underlying models. For example, OpenCodeInterpreter demonstrates higher robustness against certain attacks due to hard-coded constraints and environmental sandboxing, such as strict disk space protection. In contrast, frameworks like CodeAct exhibit lower intrinsic security awareness. The choice of the foundational LLM also plays a pivotal role; [Guo_2024_Redcode] notes that instruction fine-tuning specifically for agentic tasks can inadvertently compromise the model's safety guardrails, leading to alarmingly low rejection rates for malicious instructions. As these agents become more deeply integrated into CI/CD pipelines and developer environments, the risk of them being manipulated to execute harmful system commands, exfiltrate sensitive source code, or facilitate "living off the land" attacks [Noever_2024_AI] becomes a pressing, real-world concern. Securing agentic AI will require robust, isolated sandboxing, continuous runtime monitoring of agent actions, and alignment techniques tailored specifically for interactive, stateful environments.

### Multimodal Threats

While the vast majority of current adversarial research in the code domain focuses on text-based prompt injection and jailbreaking, the rapid emergence of multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) introduces novel threat vectors that remain largely unexplored. Multimodal threats leverage non-textual inputs—such as images, architectural diagrams, flowcharts, or even audio—to bypass text-centric safety filters. 

In a software development context, an attacker could theoretically embed malicious code logic or prompt injection payloads within a seemingly benign architecture diagram or a screenshot of an error message. When the developer prompts the MLLM to generate code based on this visual input, the model may inadvertently process the hidden adversarial payload, resulting in the generation of vulnerable or malicious code. Because current alignment and defense mechanisms are predominantly optimized for parsing and sanitizing textual prompts, they are largely blind to adversarial payloads hidden in other modalities. As code models increasingly incorporate multimodal capabilities to assist with tasks like UI-to-code generation, visual debugging, or interpreting legacy system diagrams, addressing these cross-modal threats will become imperative. Future research must pioneer cross-modal defense strategies capable of analyzing and sanitizing inputs across all supported modalities, ensuring that the semantic intent of the prompt remains safe regardless of its format.

### Scalability of Defenses

Developing defense mechanisms that can scale commensurately with the rapid advancement, increasing parameter size, and expanding context windows of LLMs is a significant open challenge. Many current defense strategies, such as comprehensive adversarial training or manual red-teaming, are highly resource-intensive and struggle to keep pace with the rapidly evolving landscape of adversarial tactics. 

[Nie_2024_Secodeplt] proposes a pragmatic two-stage data creation pipeline to address the scalability bottleneck in generating high-quality training data for secure models. By combining manually curated, high-quality seed examples with automated, LLM-driven mutation techniques, this approach attempts to achieve both quality and scale. However, as attackers increasingly employ sophisticated, automated, and multi-step tactics [Muntasir_2025_Mocha], static defenses quickly become obsolete. Defenses must evolve to become more dynamic and scalable. This necessitates the development of automated, AI-driven red-teaming frameworks capable of continuously probing models for zero-day vulnerabilities at scale. Additionally, there is a pressing need for lightweight, inference-time defenses—such as input perplexity filtering or activation monitoring—that can detect and neutralize attacks without introducing prohibitive latency or computational overhead, ensuring that defenses can scale effectively across diverse deployment environments.

### Future Research Directions

The landscape of adversarial attacks on code models is highly dynamic, necessitating continuous, forward-looking innovation in defense strategies. Based on the current state of the art, several critical areas for future research emerge:

First, there is an urgent need for more resilient alignment techniques capable of defending against complex, multi-step, and context-aware adversarial tactics [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Current alignment methods often fail when faced with sophisticated jailbreaks that distribute malicious intent across multiple turns of a conversation.

Second, research must expand beyond the analysis of isolated code snippets to consider the broader, systemic context of software development workflows. This includes investigating vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation (RACG) systems, where maliciously injected code in retrieved, third-party repositories can silently compromise the generated output [Lin_2025_LLMs]. It also requires exploring the risks associated with collaborative coding environments, where attackers might introduce subtle, semantics-preserving transformations to evade manual code review while introducing vulnerabilities [Storek_2025_AI].

Third, the development of standardized, comprehensive, and continuously updated benchmarks for evaluating the security and robustness of code models is essential. These benchmarks must move beyond simple text-based jailbreaks to encompass a wide range of attack vectors, including agentic manipulation and multimodal threats, providing a holistic assessment of a model's safety-utility trade-off.

Finally, fostering deeper collaboration between the artificial intelligence and traditional cybersecurity communities will be vital. By bridging the gap between machine learning alignment and established software security principles, the research community can anticipate emerging threats and develop robust, scalable defenses necessary to secure the future of AI-assisted software engineering.

hallucinations_factual_integrity.text:
# Hallucinations and the Integrity of LLM Outputs

Hallucination, defined as the generation of factually incorrect or contextually unsupported content, represents a primary threat to the integrity of Large Language Model (LLM) outputs [Wang_2024_Developing]. As LLMs are increasingly integrated into high-stakes environments such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and human-computer interaction, the security implications of these errors become critical, as they can lead to misinformation with irreparable consequences [Wang_2024_Mllm]. The research landscape has evolved from basic error detection in 2024 to sophisticated mechanistic auditing and domain-specific grounding by 2026 [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v4]. This section investigates the security implications of hallucinations, treating them as a fundamental vulnerability in the reliability of generative systems.

### Mechanisms of Multimodal Hallucinations

In Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), hallucinations manifest as contradictions between visual inputs and textual outputs [Wang_2024_Mllm]. A significant challenge identified in 2024 is the "language prior" problem, where models over-rely on textual training biases while ignoring visual evidence [Wang_2024_Mllm, Xing_2024_Mitigating]. This phenomenon, also termed "Text Inertia," stems from architectural paradigms that map visual representations onto text tokens, leading the model to prioritize linguistic probability over visual grounding [Wang_2024_Mllm]. 

Mechanistic studies have revealed that while MLLMs often recognize visual objects in preceding layers (layers 1-11), these signals are suppressed by strong knowledge priors in deeper layers [Wang_2024_Mllm]. The "Aggregation Pattern" further exacerbates this, where visual information is aggregated to specific anchor tokens, causing the model to ignore broader visual context during sequence generation [Wang_2024_Mllm]. To mitigate these issues, researchers introduced methods like Dynamic Correction decoding (DeCo), which adaptively integrates knowledge from preceding layers to adjust output logits [Wang_2024_Mllm]. Similarly, Visual Amplification Fusion (VAF) was proposed in 2025 to enhance attention to visual signals in middle layers where modality fusion occurs, reducing bias without increasing inference latency [Yin_2025_Clearsight]. For clinical settings, deterministic methods such as Confidence-Evidence Bayesian Gain (CEBaG) utilize token-level predictive variance and evidence magnitude to detect hallucinations without the need for expensive stochastic sampling [Asadi_2024_Deterministic].

### Evolution of Auditing: From NLI to Rubric-based Judges

The detection of factual inconsistencies has transitioned through several paradigms. In 2024, Natural Language Inference (NLI) emerged as a dominant framework for checking factual consistency [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative]. Early systems like MiniCheck-FT5 demonstrated that small NLI models (770M parameters) could achieve GPT-4 level accuracy by training on synthetic data generated through Claim-to-Doc (C2D) and Doc-to-Claim (D2C) methods [Tang_2024_LLMs]. These methods decompose human claims into atomic facts and generate supporting or non-supporting documents to create challenging entailment pairs [Tang_2024_LLMs].

However, research by Jing et al. (2024) indicated that zero-shot LLMs, particularly GPT-4, often outperform standard NLI models like HHEM in capturing both intrinsic (contradictory) and extrinsic (additive) hallucinations [Jing_2024_Scale]. This led to the development of rubric-based evaluation templates, where LLMs act as judges to score faithfulness across dimensions such as factual consistency, knowledge congruence, and style alignment [Jing_2024_Scale]. To support these evaluations, comprehensive benchmarks like FaithEval and HaluBench were established, providing thousands of contextual QA pairs across diverse domains to test model sensitivity to unanswerable and counterfactual contexts [Ming_2024_Faitheval, Sunitha_2024_Lynx].

### The 2025 Trend: Specialized Small-scale Grounding Models

A pivotal shift occurred in 2025, as researchers challenged the necessity of massive proprietary models for hallucination detection. The emergence of specialized models in the 3.8B to 8B parameter range, such as Paladin-mini, Humains-Junior, and HDM-2, demonstrated that efficiency does not necessitate a compromise in performance [Ivry_2025_Paladin, Yaron_2025_GPT, Paudel_2025_Hallucinot]. 

Paladin-mini (3.8B) utilizes a formal mathematical framework based on "Minimal Support" conditions, ensuring that every piece of evidence in a grounding set is essential for the claim [Ivry_2025_Paladin]. Similarly, Humains-Junior (3.8B) introduced "Exoskeleton Reasoning," a cognitive scaffold that enforces epistemic discipline by prioritizing provided context over internal model beliefs [Yaron_2025_GPT]. This approach achieved a 19x reduction in inference costs compared to GPT-4o while maintaining equivalent grounding performance [Yaron_2025_GPT]. For enterprise applications, the HDM-2 model (3B) employs a multi-task architecture that probes internal hidden layers to validate common knowledge and provides granular word-level annotations for detected hallucinations [Paudel_2025_Hallucinot]. These developments highlight a move toward "epistemic restraint," where models are fine-tuned for protocol compliance rather than just domain-specific facts [Yaron_2025_GPT].

### Domain-Specific Faithfulness and Expert-in-the-Loop Systems

General-purpose models often struggle with the specialized requirements of fields like healthcare and climate science. In the medical domain, the MEDHALU benchmark was introduced to study hallucinations in real-world healthcare queries [Agarwal_2024_Medhalu]. To improve detection, researchers proposed expert-in-the-loop strategies that integrate human reasoning—such as cross-referencing trusted medical resources—directly into LLM prompts [Agarwal_2024_Medhalu]. For biomedical summarization, the PlainQAFact metric was developed to evaluate "elaborative explanations," which introduce external but factually correct context to improve lay comprehension [You_2025_Plainqafact].

In climate science, the development of ClimateGPT Faithful+ demonstrated that faithfulness could be improved by identifying and ablating unfaithful subsets of training data, such as non-expert grounded examples [Thulke_2025_Listen]. This model improved the support rate for atomic claims from 30% to 57% by focusing on high-faithfulness, closed-ended examples [Thulke_2025_Listen]. Furthermore, the introduction of CogniBench in 2025 expanded the scope of evaluation to include "cognitive statements," which require making inferences from context rather than simple rephrasing [Tang_2025_Cognibench].

### Advanced Verification Architectures and Multi-Agent Collaboration

By 2026, the field moved toward self-regulating, multi-stage architectures to ensure factual integrity. Haque et al. (2026) proposed a four-phase tiered retrieval system using LangGraph, which includes intrinsic early-exit logic, adaptive search routing to trusted databases, and extrinsic atomic claim-level verification [Haque_2026_LLM]. This framework identifies critical failure modes such as "False-Premise Overclaiming" and "Retrieval Distraction" [Haque_2026_LLM].

Multi-agent frameworks like InEx and HalluDetect further automate hallucination mitigation. InEx utilizes internal introspective reasoning guided by entropy-based uncertainty estimation, followed by external cross-modal collaboration between editing and self-reflection agents [Yang_2025_Inex]. HalluDetect addresses the "Domain Reliance Paradox" in RAG-based conversational systems by filtering out benign conversational inferences that might otherwise be misclassified as hallucinations [Anaokar_2025_Halludetect]. These systems represent a transition toward white-box auditing, exemplified by innovations like LatentAudit, which uses residual-stream geometry for real-time, privacy-preserving verification [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v4].

### Conclusion

The evolution of hallucination research reflects a deepening understanding of LLM vulnerabilities. From identifying the language prior problem in MLLMs [Wang_2024_Mllm] to the deployment of specialized small-scale models [Ivry_2025_Paladin, Yaron_2025_GPT] and multi-agent verification pipelines [Yang_2025_Inex, Haque_2026_LLM], the focus has shifted from simple detection to proactive mitigation and mechanistic transparency. As LLMs continue to expand into multilingual and hyper-local contexts [Islam_2025_LLMs, Gao_2025_AI], maintaining factual integrity remains a cornerstone of LLM security.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.text:
# Introduction

## AI Security Paradigm Shift
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) into critical infrastructure, healthcare, finance, and everyday consumer applications has precipitated a profound paradigm shift in the cybersecurity landscape. Historically, information security has focused on deterministic vulnerabilities within software systems—such as buffer overflows, cross-site scripting, and SQL injections—where the logic is explicitly programmed and flaws can be patched through code revisions. However, the advent of deep learning and, more recently, Large Language Models (LLMs), has introduced a fundamentally different class of vulnerabilities. AI systems are not programmed but trained; their behavior emerges from complex, high-dimensional statistical representations learned from vast datasets. 

This shift from deterministic logic to probabilistic inference has given rise to AI-specific security threats, most notably adversarial attacks. In this new paradigm, adversaries do not necessarily exploit traditional software bugs; instead, they manipulate the inputs or the training data to subvert the model's intended behavior. The opacity of deep neural networks exacerbates this issue, making it exceedingly difficult to guarantee robustness or interpret the root causes of failures. Consequently, securing AI systems requires a departure from conventional cybersecurity frameworks, demanding novel methodologies that address the inherent vulnerabilities of statistical learning models.

## Threat Landscape Evolution
As AI technologies have advanced, the threat landscape has evolved in tandem, growing in both complexity and scale. Early research in adversarial machine learning primarily concentrated on the computer vision domain, demonstrating how imperceptible perturbations to images could cause state-of-the-art classifiers to make glaring errors. Techniques such as the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) established the foundational understanding of evasion attacks. However, the threat landscape has since expanded far beyond simple image classification.

With the proliferation of generative AI and LLMs, adversaries have developed sophisticated techniques tailored to natural language and code generation. Modern language models, despite being equipped with safety mechanisms and guardrails, remain susceptible to novel attack vectors. For instance, recent studies have demonstrated that these defenses can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking strategies, utilizing carefully crafted prompts that exploit model vulnerabilities to elicit malicious or restricted outputs [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Furthermore, the deployment of LLMs as coding assistants has introduced critical security risks. Attackers can leverage these systems to generate malicious payloads or bypass traditional guardrails by embedding contextual cues that trick the model into compliance [Noever_2024_AI]. 

Another emerging threat is generalized adversarial code-suggestions, a class of attacks derived from neural backdoors where an adversary poisons the training data so that the model generates vulnerable or malicious code only in the presence of a specific trigger pattern [Rubel_2024_LLM]. To systematically evaluate and mitigate these evolving threats, researchers are developing comprehensive benchmarks, such as the Multi-turn rObust Code BencHmArk (MOCHA), designed to expose vulnerabilities across diverse threat categories [Muntasir_2025_Mocha].

## Survey Scope
Given the rapid evolution of adversarial threats, there is a pressing need to synthesize the current state of research and provide a structured understanding of the vulnerabilities inherent in modern AI systems. The scope of this survey is to offer a comprehensive and up-to-date analysis of adversarial attacks, with a particular emphasis on the recent paradigm shift towards Large Language Models and generative AI. While previous surveys have extensively covered adversarial examples in computer vision, this work pivots to address the unique challenges posed by natural language processing, code generation, and multimodal systems.

We systematically review the latest attack methodologies, including prompt injection, jailbreaking [Muntasir_2025_Mocha], data poisoning, and backdoor attacks in code-completion systems [Rubel_2024_LLM]. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical underpinnings of these vulnerabilities and evaluate the efficacy of current defensive strategies and robustness benchmarks. By focusing on the intersection of generative AI and adversarial machine learning, this survey aims to bridge the gap between theoretical attack frameworks and practical security implications in real-world deployments. We delimit our scope by excluding traditional software vulnerabilities that do not directly exploit the statistical nature of the machine learning models themselves.

## Paper Organization
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows to provide a logical progression through the complex landscape of AI security. Section 2 establishes the foundational background, defining key concepts in adversarial machine learning and outlining the threat models considered in this survey. Section 3 presents a comprehensive taxonomy of modern adversarial attacks, categorizing them by the targeted modality (e.g., text, code, vision) and the phase of the ML lifecycle they exploit (training versus inference). 

In Section 4, we delve into the specific vulnerabilities of LLMs and AI-driven coding assistants, detailing state-of-the-art jailbreaking techniques and backdoor attacks [Noever_2024_AI, Rubel_2024_LLM]. Section 5 reviews current defensive mechanisms, mitigation strategies, and the role of comprehensive evaluation benchmarks like MOCHA [Muntasir_2025_Mocha] in assessing model robustness. Section 6 discusses the open challenges and outlines promising directions for future research in developing secure and resilient AI systems. Finally, Section 7 concludes the survey, summarizing the key findings and emphasizing the critical need for proactive security measures in the era of generative AI.

llm_hallucinations.title: Output-Level Vulnerabilities: LLM Hallucinations
llm_hallucinations.text:
# Output-Level Vulnerabilities: LLM Hallucinations

The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various domains has been accompanied by a significant and persistent challenge: hallucinations. Hallucinations occur when an LLM generates text that is factually incorrect, nonsensical, or unfaithful to the provided source material. This phenomenon undermines the reliability and trustworthiness of LLM applications, particularly in high-stakes environments such as healthcare, legal analysis, and automated decision-making systems. Understanding, detecting, and mitigating these output-level vulnerabilities is a critical area of ongoing research.

A widely adopted taxonomy categorizes hallucinations into two primary types: intrinsic and extrinsic [Wang_2024_Developing]. Intrinsic hallucinations occur when the generated output directly contradicts the provided input or source material. For example, if a prompt states that a meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, and the LLM summarizes the text by stating the meeting is on Wednesday, this is an intrinsic hallucination. Conversely, extrinsic hallucinations occur when the LLM generates information that cannot be verified by the provided input. This often happens when the model relies on its pre-trained parametric knowledge to fill in gaps, producing statements that may be factually true in the real world but are unsupported by the specific context provided to the model. Both types pose significant challenges, but they require different detection and mitigation strategies.

## Hallucination Detection

The fundamental challenge in addressing LLM hallucinations lies in accurately detecting them. As models become more sophisticated, their hallucinations often become more subtle and plausible, making them difficult for both human evaluators and automated systems to identify. The research community has developed a variety of approaches to tackle this problem, ranging from reference-based metrics to reference-free evaluation pipelines.

Traditional approaches to hallucination detection often relied on simple overlap metrics such as ROUGE or BLEU, which compare the generated text to a reference text. However, these metrics are notoriously poor at capturing semantic meaning and factual accuracy. A model might generate a sentence that has high lexical overlap with the reference but completely reverses the meaning (e.g., changing "is" to "is not"). Consequently, the field has shifted towards more semantic and reasoning-aware detection methods.

Recent advancements have introduced comprehensive pipelines designed to evaluate hallucinations without relying on gold-standard reference texts. For instance, the HalluCounter pipeline [Urlana_2025_LLM] represents a reference-free approach that extracts features from the query-response pair to determine the likelihood of hallucination. These systems often employ a multi-step process: first, extracting verifiable claims from the generated text; second, retrieving relevant evidence (either from the provided context or an external knowledge base); and third, verifying the claims against the evidence.

## NLI Models for Hallucination Detection

Natural Language Inference (NLI) has emerged as a foundational technique for detecting hallucinations, particularly in the context of faithfulness and factual consistency. NLI models are trained to determine the relationship between a premise (the source text) and a hypothesis (the generated text). The relationship is typically classified into three categories: entailment (the premise supports the hypothesis), contradiction (the premise contradicts the hypothesis), or neutral (the premise neither supports nor contradicts the hypothesis).

In the context of hallucination detection, NLI models are used to verify whether the claims made by an LLM are entailed by the provided source material. If a claim is contradicted by the source, it is flagged as an intrinsic hallucination. If the relationship is neutral, it may indicate an extrinsic hallucination, as the claim is unsupported by the context.

Researchers have developed specialized NLI models tailored for hallucination detection. For example, [Wang_2024_Developing] describes the development of a detection model by fine-tuning a pre-trained DeBERTa encoder on a diverse set of document-summary pairs. To improve the model's robustness, they incorporated a document-sentence dataset and utilized GPT-4 to label data from various public and internal sources. This fine-tuning process allows the NLI model to better understand the nuances of LLM-generated text and the specific ways in which models hallucinate.

However, traditional NLI models often operate on a pairwise sentence level, which can be computationally expensive when evaluating long documents or complex reasoning chains. To address this, more efficient approaches have been proposed. For instance, [Tang_2025_Cognibench] introduces CogniDet, an 8B-parameter model fine-tuned on an auto-labeled corpus. This model achieves high performance (70.3% F1 score) with a single forward pass, making it significantly cheaper and faster than traditional NLI baselines that require exhaustive pairwise sentence comparisons. This shift towards more efficient, single-pass detection models is crucial for scaling hallucination detection to real-world applications.

## RAG Partial Support and Fine-Grained Verification

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are frequently employed to mitigate hallucinations by grounding the LLM's responses in external, retrieved knowledge. In a typical RAG setup, the system retrieves relevant documents based on the user's query and provides them to the LLM as context. The LLM is then instructed to generate an answer based solely on the provided documents.

While RAG significantly reduces hallucinations, it introduces a new challenge: verifying the faithfulness of the generated response to the retrieved citations. Early approaches to citation evaluation treated faithfulness as a binary classification problem: a citation either supported the statement or it did not [Zhang_2024_Comparative]. However, this binary approach fails to capture the complexity of real-world generation, where a statement might be only partially supported by the cited evidence.

Recent research has emphasized the need for fine-grained citation support evaluation. [Zhang_2024_Comparative] and [Zhang_2024_Fine] highlight the limitations of binary metrics and advocate for a more nuanced categorization. They utilize datasets like VeJudge and GenSearch, which comprise thousands of statement-citation pairs annotated by human assessors. In these datasets, citations are categorized into three levels of support: full support, partial support, or no support.

Partial support occurs when a citation provides evidence for some aspects of the generated statement but fails to corroborate the entire claim. For example, if an LLM generates the statement, "The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 and is 330 meters tall," and the cited document only mentions the completion year, the citation provides only partial support. Recognizing and quantifying partial support is essential for accurately assessing the reliability of RAG systems.

The challenge of verifying direct support is further complicated when the evidence passage itself is complex or ambiguous. As noted by [Thulke_2025_Listen], claim verification pipelines often assume that if a claim is directly expressed in the given passage, its content can be considered truth. However, evaluating faithfulness requires moving beyond simple direct extraction to understanding the broader context and the nuances of partial support. Developing automated metrics that can reliably distinguish between full, partial, and no support remains an active area of research, requiring models capable of deep semantic understanding and complex reasoning.

## White-Box Detection: SVD and Internal Representations

The majority of hallucination detection methods, including NLI and RAG verification, operate as black-box approaches. They analyze the final text output of the LLM without access to the model's internal workings. While effective, black-box methods are limited by the information present in the generated text.

White-box detection methods, on the other hand, leverage the LLM's internal representations—such as hidden states, attention weights, and token probabilities—to identify hallucinations. These approaches operate on the premise that the model's internal state differs when it is generating factual information versus when it is hallucinating.

Several techniques have been developed to exploit these internal signals. As summarized by [Urlana_2025_LLM], approaches include training classifiers on the LLM's hidden representations, weighting the model's expertise, calculating token probabilities, and measuring semantic consistency across various layers.

A particularly promising white-box technique involves analyzing the hidden states using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Research by [Du_2024_LLM] and [Park_2025_LLM] focuses on detecting hallucinations by examining the model's embeddings rather than relying solely on the output text. [Du_2024_LLM] formalizes the hallucination detection problem by harnessing unlabeled LLM generations in the wild. They present a novel scoring function based on a "hallucination subspace" extracted from the model's hidden states using SVD.

The core idea is that the hidden states associated with hallucinated tokens occupy a distinct subspace compared to factual tokens. By applying SVD to a matrix of hidden states collected during generation, researchers can identify the principal components that capture the variance associated with hallucinations. The projection of a new hidden state onto this hallucination subspace can then be used as a score to predict the likelihood of hallucination.

This white-box approach offers several advantages. First, it can detect hallucinations at the token level as they are being generated, potentially allowing for real-time intervention or correction. Second, it does not require external reference texts or complex NLI models, making it computationally efficient during inference. Finally, by analyzing the model's internal representations, white-box methods can provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of hallucination, contributing to the development of more robust and reliable LLMs.

## Domain-Specific Hallucinations

While general-purpose hallucination detection methods are valuable, the nature and impact of hallucinations can vary significantly across different domains. An LLM might perform well on general knowledge tasks but hallucinate frequently when tasked with specialized domains such as medicine, law, or specific industry applications. Consequently, there is a growing need for domain-specific hallucination detection and mitigation strategies.

Domain-specific hallucinations often arise because the LLM lacks sufficient specialized knowledge in its pre-training data or because the domain requires a higher standard of factual accuracy and precise terminology. For example, in the travel domain, an LLM might hallucinate non-existent hotels, incorrect flight times, or fabricated tourist attractions.

[Jing_2024_Scale] investigated hallucinations in the travel industry by evaluating five popular LLMs on four travel-domain datasets. They proposed a rubric-based template to use LLMs as evaluators for faithfulness in Natural Language Generation (NLG). Their findings indicate that in a zero-shot setting, advanced LLMs like GPT-4 can outperform specialized NLI models (such as HHEM) in capturing both intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations within this specific domain. However, they also noted that fine-tuning NLI models on synthetic domain-specific data can significantly improve their performance.

In the realm of Question Answering (QA), the types of hallucinations can also be highly specific to the dataset. [Park_2025_LLM] evaluated their white-box detection method on four publicly available generative QA tasks: TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, SciQ, and NQ Open. Each of these datasets presents unique challenges. TruthfulQA, for instance, specifically assesses a model's robustness against generating false or unsupported answers that mimic human misconceptions. SciQ focuses on scientific facts, requiring precise terminology and domain knowledge. The performance of hallucination detection methods can vary across these datasets, highlighting the importance of evaluating models on diverse, domain-specific benchmarks.

To address domain-specific challenges, supervised approaches often leverage annotated datasets to train specialized classifiers. As noted by [Paudel_2025_Hallucinot], models like FAVA (a retrieval-augmented language model) are designed to detect and correct fine-grained hallucinations by fine-tuning on expert models and synthetic data. By tailoring the training data and detection mechanisms to the specific characteristics of a domain, researchers can develop more accurate and reliable systems for identifying and mitigating LLM hallucinations in specialized applications.

In conclusion, addressing output-level vulnerabilities caused by LLM hallucinations requires a multifaceted approach. While NLI models provide a strong foundation for semantic verification, the complexities of RAG systems necessitate fine-grained evaluation of partial support. Furthermore, the development of white-box detection methods using techniques like SVD offers promising new avenues for identifying hallucinations by analyzing the model's internal state. Finally, recognizing the unique challenges posed by domain-specific applications is crucial for developing robust and reliable LLM systems capable of operating safely in high-stakes environments.

prompt_injection_agentic_systems.title: Prompt Injection in Autonomous and Reasoning Systems
prompt_injection_agentic_systems.text:
## Prompt Injection in Autonomous and Reasoning Systems

The research landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) security has undergone a rapid and sophisticated evolution between 2024 and 2026, transitioning from the discovery of basic structural vulnerabilities to the exploitation of complex, autonomous agentic environments [l2_Prompt Injection_v102]. While early research focused on direct prompt injection (PI) within chatbot interfaces, the integration of LLMs into agentic workflows—where models interact with external tools, web environments, and internal reasoning traces—has introduced novel attack surfaces. This section analyzes the shift toward structural obfuscation, the rise of Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in multi-modal systems, and the unique security challenges posed by Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs).

### Structural Obfuscation and Formatting Vulnerabilities

In 2024, research primarily characterized PI through structural and formatting exploits that leveraged the autoregressive nature of LLMs. A foundational example is 'FlipAttack,' which disguises harmful intents by flipping the order of words or characters [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. This method exploits the left-to-right reading nature of LLMs to bypass guardrails, achieving a 98% attack success rate (ASR) on GPT-4o by providing 'denoising' guidance that instructs the model to reconstruct and execute the hidden command [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. Similarly, the 'SQL Injection Jailbreak' (SIJ) draws a functional analogy to second-order SQL injection by manipulating prompt structures to 'comment out' system-defined assistant prefixes [Zhao_2024_SQL]. By inserting replicated starting markers and pattern-control instructions, SIJ achieved near 100% ASR on open-source models and over 85% on closed-source models like GPT-4o-mini [Zhao_2024_SQL, Zhao_2024_SQL].

Beyond simple character manipulation, 'LogiBreak' demonstrated that shifting the token distribution away from aligned natural language spaces can evade safety filters [Peng_2025_LLM]. By transforming harmful requests into formal logical expressions (First-Order Logic), attackers exploit the gap where models are trained to refuse specific natural language patterns but lack robust semantic alignment for formal logic representations [Peng_2025_LLM]. These structural attacks highlight a fundamental vulnerability: safety alignment often relies on token-level cues rather than deep semantic understanding.

### Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in Agentic Environments

As LLMs transitioned into autonomous agents, the focus shifted to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), where malicious instructions are embedded in external data retrieved by the model [l2_Prompt Injection_v102, Zhu_2025_AI]. Unlike direct attacks, IPI redirects agents to take unauthorized actions—such as exfiltrating data or executing terminal commands—without direct user intervention [Zhu_2025_AI].

#### Web Navigation and Multi-modal Injection
Autonomous web agents are particularly susceptible to IPI via adversarial content embedded in HTML. Research has identified eight distinct HTML-based injection techniques, including the use of non-visible elements like meta tags, ARIA labels, and opacity-zero `<div>` tags to bypass text-based sanitization [Verma_2025_LLMs]. In 2025, 'WebInject' introduced a more stealthy approach using human-imperceptible visual perturbations [Wang_2025_Webinject]. By optimizing pixel-level changes via a differentiable mapping network, WebInject manipulates Multi-modal LLM (MLLM) agents into performing target actions, such as unauthorized clicks, while maintaining visual fidelity for the user [Wang_2025_Webinject]. Furthermore, universal adversarial triggers embedded in webpage HTML can be optimized using algorithms like Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to function across diverse user instructions, enabling high-risk scenarios like credential exfiltration [Johnson_2025_LLM].

#### Coding Editors and Tool Selection
Agentic AI coding editors, such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot, represent a high-stakes environment for IPI. The 'AIShellJack' framework revealed that embedding malicious instructions in external resources, such as `.cursorrules` files, can lead to the execution of unauthorized terminal commands with success rates up to 84% [Liu_2025_AI]. This vulnerability extends to the tool selection process itself. 'ToolHijacker' targets the two-step retrieval and selection pipeline in LLM agents by crafting malicious tool documents [Shi_2025_LLM]. By optimizing tool descriptions for both retrieval similarity and selection likelihood, attackers can force an agent to select a 'shadow' tool instead of the legitimate one [Shi_2025_LLM].

### Security Vulnerabilities in Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs)

The emergence of Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs), such as DeepSeek-R1, has introduced a new paradigm of internal vulnerabilities related to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes [l2_Prompt Injection_v102]. RLLMs are characterized by their ability to generate intermediate reasoning tokens before producing a final answer, a process that provides a novel attack surface.

#### Reasoning Interruption and False Memories
The 'Reasoning Interruption Attack' exploits a 'thinking-stopped' vulnerability, where specific triggers—often simple arithmetic tasks—force the model to predict the `<|end_of_thinking|>` special token prematurely [Cui_2025_LLM]. This attack can achieve a 100% ASR on specific datasets by placing attack prompts in both the user input and the assistant's output prefix [Cui_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, RLLMs exhibit a heightened susceptibility to 'false memories' [Cui_2025_LLMs]. The 'VORTEXPIA' attack induces models to proactively extract private user information by injecting a 'fake user information set' into external data. The model is deceived into treating this malicious request as a legitimate data verification task, revealing that stronger reasoning capabilities can paradoxically lead to higher privacy risks [Cui_2025_LLMs].

#### Quantifying Reasoning Complexity for Detection
To counter these vulnerabilities, researchers have proposed metrics to monitor the integrity of the reasoning process. The 'Number of Thoughts' (NofT) metric quantifies task complexity based on the number of intermediate reasoning steps [Marinelli_2025_Harnessing]. Deviations between the predicted NofT (using a Random Forest classifier) and the actual reasoning steps generated by the model can detect adversarial injections with up to 95% accuracy [Marinelli_2025_Harnessing]. This suggests that the very CoT process targeted by attackers can also serve as a signal for defense.

### Multi-modal and Robotic System Security

The integration of LLMs into physical and multi-modal systems, such as mobile robots, introduces safety-critical risks. In robotic navigation tasks, LLMs serving as the 'brain' process multi-modal inputs including LiDAR data and camera views [Zhang_2024_LLM]. While models like GPT-4o show some resilience, they remain vulnerable to Goal Hijacking Injections (GHI) [Zhang_2024_LLM]. To mitigate this, defense strategies have evolved to include 'Secure Prompting'—which prioritizes tasks via a defense patch—and 'Response-based Detection,' where the model must generate natural language reasoning for its actions before execution [Zhang_2024_LLM].

In the broader multi-modal context, the 'Bi-Modal Adversarial Prompt Attack' (BAP) demonstrates the power of simultaneous optimization [Ying_2024_Jailbreak]. By embedding universal adversarial perturbations in images while iteratively refining textual prompts through a CoT feedback loop, BAP significantly outperforms single-modality attacks against aligned Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) [Ying_2024_Jailbreak, Ying_2024_Jailbreak].

### Automated Discovery and Defense-in-Depth

The scale of agentic environments has necessitated the development of automated evaluation frameworks. 'AGENTVIGIL' utilizes blackbox fuzzing and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to automatically discover IPI vulnerabilities in agents, nearly doubling the effectiveness of handcrafted prompts [Wang_2025_LLM]. Similarly, the 'WASP' benchmark provides a realistic threat model for web agents, identifying a phenomenon of 'security by incompetence' where agents are easily hijacked but often fail to complete complex multi-step malicious goals [Evtimov_2025_Wasp].

Defensive research is maturing toward internal activation steering and architectural mitigations [l2_Prompt Injection_v102]. The 'MELON' framework (Masked re-Execution and TooL comparisON) detects IPI by re-executing an agent's trajectory with a masked user prompt [Zhu_2025_AI]. If the actions generated in the original and masked executions remain similar, it indicates the agent is following an injected instruction rather than the user's intent [Zhu_2025_AI]. Other proposed defenses include 'Self-Reminder-Key,' which appends random tokens to disrupt pattern matching [Zhao_2024_SQL], and 'TopicAttack' mitigation strategies that focus on maintaining attention on the original instruction [Chen_2025_Topicattack]. As of 2026, the field is moving toward domain-specific benchmarks, such as the Medical Prompt Injection Benchmark (MPIB), to quantify real-world harm in specialized sectors [l2_Prompt Injection_v102].

prompt_injection_jailbreaking.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
prompt_injection_jailbreaking.text:
# Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking

The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications has exposed a critical frontier in artificial intelligence security: inference-time threats. Unlike training-time vulnerabilities such as data poisoning or backdoor insertion, inference-time threats exploit the fundamental mechanisms by which a fully trained model processes and responds to user inputs. At the core of these vulnerabilities are prompt injection and jailbreaking. While these terms are sometimes used interchangeably, they represent distinct paradigms of attack. Prompt injection typically involves subverting a model's original instructions by embedding malicious commands within user-provided data, causing the model to execute unintended actions. Jailbreaking, on the other hand, refers to the deliberate crafting of inputs designed to bypass the model's built-in safety guardrails, coercing it into generating restricted, harmful, or unethical content. 

As LLMs have become more sophisticated, so too have the techniques used to compromise them. Early jailbreaking attempts relied heavily on manual prompt engineering—users intuitively crafting hypothetical scenarios, role-playing prompts, or complex logical puzzles to trick the model. However, the landscape has rapidly evolved towards systematic, automated, and structurally complex attack vectors. This section delves into the mechanics of these advanced inference-time threats, exploring black-box jailbreaking, structural manipulations, automated adversarial generation, the AutoDAN framework, and the emerging vulnerabilities within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.

## Black-box Jailbreaking

In the context of LLM security, threat models are generally categorized based on the attacker's level of access to the target system. White-box attacks assume full access to the model's architecture, weights, gradients, and training data, allowing for highly optimized, gradient-based adversarial perturbations. However, the most powerful and widely used commercial LLMs are deployed behind proprietary APIs, restricting users to black-box access. In a black-box scenario, the attacker can only interact with the model by submitting inputs and observing the generated outputs, with no visibility into the internal workings of the system.

Black-box jailbreaking represents a significant challenge for attackers, as they cannot rely on gradient descent to optimize their malicious prompts. Instead, they must employ heuristic search strategies, exploit transferability from open-source models, or utilize iterative querying techniques to probe the model's decision boundaries. The primary constraint in black-box attacks is the cost and efficiency of the attack. Commercial APIs impose rate limits and charge per token, making brute-force approaches economically and practically unfeasible. Consequently, modern black-box jailbreaking research focuses on maximizing the attack success rate while minimizing the number of queries required.

The success of black-box jailbreaking highlights a fundamental tension in LLM alignment: the balance between helpfulness and harmlessness. Models are heavily fine-tuned using techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to refuse harmful requests. However, because they are also trained to be maximally helpful and follow user instructions, attackers can exploit this instruction-following imperative by framing malicious requests in ways that circumvent the safety filters. This often involves obfuscation, context switching, or exploiting the model's cognitive blind spots, leading to the development of structural manipulation techniques.

## Structural Manipulations

Structural manipulations constitute a class of jailbreaking techniques that alter the format, syntax, or structural presentation of a prompt without changing its underlying semantic intent. The goal is to present the malicious request in a configuration that the model's safety filters fail to recognize as harmful, yet the core language modeling capabilities can still parse and execute. This approach exploits the discrepancy between how safety classifiers evaluate text and how autoregressive language models process it.

A prominent example of structural manipulation is FlipAttack [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. This method introduces a simple yet highly effective black-box jailbreak by exploiting the autoregressive nature of LLMs. Autoregressive models generate text sequentially, predicting the next token based on the preceding context. Consequently, they exhibit a strong left-to-right processing bias; their understanding of a sequence is heavily dependent on the initial tokens. FlipAttack leverages this insight by disguising the malicious prompt through structural alterations, specifically by introducing noise or flipping the text on the left side of the input [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. 

The mechanism behind FlipAttack reveals a critical vulnerability in how LLMs comprehend text. When noise is added to the beginning of a sentence, the model struggles to holistically comprehend the malicious intent, effectively blinding the safety mechanisms that rely on recognizing clear, harmful patterns. However, because the core semantic tokens remain present (albeit structurally obfuscated), the model's generative engine can still piece together the request and produce the targeted harmful output. 

The superiority of structural manipulations like FlipAttack lies in their efficiency and stealth. FlipAttack can successfully jailbreak state-of-the-art LLMs with only a single query, drastically reducing the attack time and API costs associated with iterative black-box methods [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. Furthermore, empirical evaluations demonstrate that FlipAttack achieves high success rates across various categories of harmful behavior, particularly excelling in domains like malware generation [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. The success of such methods underscores the limitations of current safety training, which often overfits to standard, well-formed malicious queries and fails to generalize to structurally anomalous inputs.

## Automated Adversarial Generation

As manual jailbreaking requires significant human ingenuity and trial-and-error, the natural progression for attackers has been the automation of adversarial prompt generation. Automated adversarial generation seeks to algorithmically discover inputs that reliably bypass safety filters. While early automated methods often produced strings of gibberish that could be easily detected by perplexity filters, recent advancements focus on generating adversarial suffixes or prompts that are semantically coherent and natural-looking.

A notable advancement in this domain is AdvPrompter [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. AdvPrompter shifts the paradigm by introducing a generative model specifically trained to produce adversarial suffixes. Unlike optimization-based methods that append nonsensical token sequences to a prompt, AdvPrompter generates suffixes that exhibit comparatively lower perplexity, meaning they closely resemble natural human language [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. This is a critical advantage, as many defense mechanisms rely on perplexity thresholds to identify and block anomalous inputs.

The architecture of AdvPrompter operates on an iterative learning loop. The generative model first produces a set of candidate adversarial suffixes. These candidates are then appended to malicious queries and evaluated against the target LLM [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. Based on the target model's responses—specifically, whether the safety filters were triggered or bypassed—the generative model updates its parameters to improve the efficacy of future candidates. This closed-loop system allows AdvPrompter to continuously refine its attack strategy, adapting to the specific vulnerabilities of the target model. By automating the discovery of low-perplexity adversarial suffixes, AdvPrompter demonstrates that automated attacks can be both highly effective and difficult to detect using standard heuristic defenses.

## AutoDAN: Genetic Algorithms in Jailbreaking

Another highly influential approach to automated jailbreaking is AutoDAN [Liu_2024_Autodan]. AutoDAN represents a significant leap in the systematic generation of adversarial prompts by employing genetic algorithms to evolve jailbreak templates. Genetic algorithms, inspired by the principles of natural selection, are particularly well-suited for navigating the complex, discrete search space of language tokens.

In the AutoDAN framework, a population of candidate jailbreak prompts is initialized. These candidates undergo a process of evaluation, selection, crossover, and mutation. During evaluation, each prompt is scored based on its ability to elicit a harmful response from the target model while maintaining a high degree of stealth (e.g., low perplexity or semantic coherence). The highest-scoring prompts are selected to act as "parents" for the next generation. Through crossover, segments of successful prompts are combined to create new offspring, while mutation introduces random alterations to individual tokens or phrases to explore new areas of the search space.

The reliance on a genetic algorithm allows AutoDAN to iteratively refine complex, multi-layered jailbreak prompts that would be nearly impossible for a human to craft manually [Liu_2024_Autodan]. Over successive generations, the algorithm converges on highly optimized prompts that exploit subtle interactions between tokens to bypass safety mechanisms. 

While AutoDAN is highly effective, it is important to contextualize it within the broader landscape of automated attacks. Other methodologies have sought to improve upon or diverge from the genetic algorithm approach. For instance, some recent frameworks employ multi-agent systems with lifelong learning designs, enabling the automatic discovery of jailbreaks through continuous interaction and adaptation, highlighting key conceptual differences from AutoDAN's evolutionary approach [Liu_2024_Autodan]. Nevertheless, AutoDAN remains a foundational benchmark in automated jailbreaking, demonstrating the power of evolutionary search techniques in compromising LLM alignment.

## RAG System Vulnerabilities

While the aforementioned techniques primarily target the direct interaction between a user and an LLM, the integration of LLMs into broader system architectures has introduced entirely new attack surfaces. One of the most significant architectural shifts in recent years is the widespread adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The public's increasing demand for LLMs to handle private domain information, access proprietary databases, and provide real-time iterative updates has necessitated the integration of external knowledge bases [Wang_2024_LLMs]. RAG addresses the inherent limitations of static model weights by dynamically retrieving relevant documents from an external corpus and appending them to the user's prompt before generation [Wang_2024_LLMs].

However, this reliance on external data sources creates a severe vulnerability known as indirect prompt injection. In a standard prompt injection attack, the user directly inputs the malicious command. In an indirect prompt injection attack against a RAG system, the attacker poisons the external knowledge base or manipulates the retrieved documents. When a legitimate user queries the system, the RAG mechanism retrieves the poisoned document and feeds it into the LLM. Because the LLM cannot inherently distinguish between the user's original instructions and the instructions embedded within the retrieved context, it may execute the malicious payload.

The consequences of RAG vulnerabilities are profound. Attackers can exploit these systems to exfiltrate sensitive information, manipulate the model's outputs to spread disinformation, or execute unauthorized actions on behalf of the user. This vulnerability is particularly acute in agentic AI systems, where the LLM is granted the ability to interact with external tools, APIs, or file systems. Research has shown that AI agents exhibit a critical vulnerability in their tendency to confuse user data with system instructions, making them highly susceptible to prompt injection attacks [Liu_2025_AI]. Through carefully crafted prompts embedded in retrieved data, attackers can override the system instructions and force the AI agent to execute arbitrary commands [Liu_2025_AI].

This vulnerability extends to advanced AI coding assistants and editors. For example, studies evaluating agentic AI coding editors have revealed significant security flaws. In certain scenarios, tools like Cursor operating in Auto mode have exhibited attack success rates as high as 83.4% when subjected to prompt injection attacks, while other integrations like GitHub Copilot demonstrate varying degrees of susceptibility depending on the underlying model [Liu_2025_AI]. These findings highlight the urgent need for robust defenses in RAG and agentic systems. 

Defending against RAG vulnerabilities requires a multi-layered approach. Current strategies are broadly divided into prevention-based and detection-based defenses [Liu_2025_AI]. Prevention mechanisms attempt to structurally isolate system instructions from retrieved data, often using strict formatting or data sanitization techniques. Detection mechanisms, on the other hand, aim to identify malicious intent within the retrieved context before it is processed by the LLM. Despite these efforts, the semantic gap between effective data retrieval and secure instruction execution remains a formidable challenge, and RAG systems continue to be a primary target for sophisticated inference-time attacks.

## Conclusion

The evolution of inference-time threats from manual prompt engineering to sophisticated, automated, and structurally complex attacks underscores the fragility of current LLM alignment techniques. Black-box jailbreaking methods demonstrate that attackers do not need access to model internals to find critical vulnerabilities. Techniques like FlipAttack show that simple structural manipulations can completely blind safety classifiers by exploiting the autoregressive nature of text generation. Meanwhile, automated frameworks like AdvPrompter and AutoDAN leverage generative models and genetic algorithms to systematically discover highly effective, low-perplexity adversarial inputs. 

Furthermore, the integration of LLMs into complex architectures like RAG systems has expanded the attack surface, introducing the severe threat of indirect prompt injection. As LLMs become increasingly autonomous and integrated into critical workflows, the distinction between user data and system instructions becomes a paramount security concern. Addressing these inference-time threats requires moving beyond superficial safety filters and developing robust, fundamental defenses that can withstand both algorithmic optimization and structural obfuscation.
